twistno equivalentengine 5.0 and elastic clustersboth lack features that engine 8.0 has on an instance-based cluster Why
trapIClientSessionHandlea transaction on Amazon DocumentDBAWS limits it to one minute, and it cannot create a collection Why
Note

How this chapter was checked. Its examples were run against a MongoDB 8.0 container on 3 October 2026, and none was run against an Amazon DocumentDB cluster. What it says about Amazon DocumentDB comes from the AWS developer guide of October 2026, for engine version 8.0 on an instance-based cluster.

A document, not a rowtwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
using MongoDB.Bson;
using MongoDB.Bson.Serialization.Attributes;

public class Order
{
    [BsonId]
    [BsonRepresentation(BsonType.ObjectId)]
    public string? Id { get; set; }

    public required Customer Customer { get; set; }
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; set; } = [];
    public OrderStatus Status { get; set; }
    public DateTime PlacedAt { get; set; } = DateTime.UtcNow;
}
Spring Data MongoDB
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.Id;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.Document;

@Document("orders")
public class Order {

    @Id
    private String id;

    private Customer customer;
    private List<OrderLine> lines;
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.NEW;
    private Instant placedAt = Instant.now();

    public Order(Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        this.customer = customer;
        this.lines = lines;
    }
}
Reading the code
@Document("orders")

Names the collection, the counterpart of a table. Each order is one document in it: the order, with its customer and lines inside.

@Id

From org.springframework.data.annotation, not from Jakarta Persistence (JPA). It maps the field to the document's _id.

private String id;

Spring Data generates an id only for a String, an ObjectId or a BigInteger, and stores it as an ObjectId, MongoDB's own kind of id. So the id is a String here, not the long of the relational chapters.

private List<OrderLine> lines;

No annotation is needed: a nested object or list is stored inside the document. What the stored document holds lists each type.

A record can be a documenttrap#

In the relational chapter, an entity could not be a record. A document can. Spring Data MongoDB creates the object itself, and its reference says: “If the type is a Java Record the canonical constructor is used.”

@Document("orders")
public record Order(@Id String id, Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines,
                    OrderStatus status, Instant placedAt) { }

@Id on a component marks the id. The rest of this chapter uses this Order.

Gotcha

Saving a record does not fill in its id. A record cannot change, so save returns a new one that carries the generated id:

var order = new Order(null, customer, lines, OrderStatus.NEW, Instant.now());
Order saved = orders.save(order);     // orders is the OrderRepository

System.out.println(order.id());       // prints null
System.out.println(saved.id());       // prints 6ac1845b71b478951620fb72

Keep working with saved. The .NET driver sets Id on the object you passed to InsertOne; that habit fails here.

Repositories and derived queriestwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
using MongoDB.Driver;

var client = new MongoClient(connectionString);
IMongoCollection<Order> orders = client
    .GetDatabase("shop")
    .GetCollection<Order>("orders");

await orders.InsertOneAsync(order);

List<Order> paid = await orders
    .Find(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Paid)
    .ToListAsync();

var filter = Builders<Order>.Filter
    .Eq(o => o.Customer.Id, "c-42");
List<Order> hers = await orders.Find(filter).ToListAsync();

List<Order> withProduct = await orders
    .Find(o => o.Lines.Any(l => l.ProductId == "A-1"))
    .ToListAsync();
Spring Data MongoDB
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.repository.MongoRepository;

public interface OrderRepository
        extends MongoRepository<Order, String> {

    // PAID sent the filter {"status": "PAID"}
    List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);

    // "c-42" sent {"customer._id": "c-42"}
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId);

    // "A-1" sent {"lines.productId": "A-1"}
    List<Order> findByLinesProductId(String productId);
}

// in a service that was given the repository
Order saved = orders.save(order);
List<Order> paid = orders.findByStatus(OrderStatus.PAID);

This is the repository of the JPA chapter again: Spring Data writes the class, and derives each query from the method's name. Each comment shows the filter that method sent in the run. A name can reach into a nested object, as CustomerId does, and into a list, as LinesProductId does.

save inserts a new document, and replaces an existing one whole. There is no MongoClient to create: Boot builds one from the connection setting.

MongoTemplate for the resttwist#

MongoDB .NET driver
var update = Builders<Order>.Update
    .Set(o => o.Status, OrderStatus.Paid);

await orders.UpdateOneAsync(o => o.Id == id, update);
Spring Data MongoDB
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Criteria.where;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Query.query;

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Update;

template.updateFirst(
        query(where("id").is(id)),
        new Update().set("status", OrderStatus.PAID),
        Order.class);
Reading the code
template.updateFirst(

template is the MongoTemplate that Boot creates, from the package org.springframework.data.mongodb.core. This call changes one field in place, where save would replace the whole document.

query(where("id").is(id)),

The counterpart of a filter builder. A field is named by a string, so the compiler does not check it. The template translates id to _id.

new Update().set("status", OrderStatus.PAID),

In the run this sent {"$set": {"status": "PAID"}}. inc, push and pull work the same way.

Embed or referencenew#

In a relational schema, an order's lines are rows in a second table. In a document database you choose, for each object an order holds. Embed it, and it is stored inside the order's document. Reference it, and the order stores only its id.

Embed what is read with its owner, and reference what lives without it. Lines are never read without their order, so they are embedded, as orders.save(order) stored them in the run:

{
  "_id": { "$oid": "6ac1845b71b478951620fb72" },
  "customer": { "_id": "c-42", "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },
  "lines": [
    { "productId": "A-1", "quantity": 2,
      "unitPrice": { "amount": { "$numberDecimal": "19.99" }, "currency": "EUR" } }
  ],
  "status": "NEW",
  "placedAt": { "$date": "2026-10-03T22:40:27.22Z" },
  "_class": "com.acme.billing.Order"
}
Reading the code
"lines": [

An array inside the order. One read returns the whole order: no join, and no lazy loading.

"customer": { "_id": "c-42", "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" },

Embedded too, as a copy made when the order was placed. A nested field named id is stored as _id.

"_class": "com.acme.billing.Order"

Spring Data adds the class name, so that it knows which type to create on reading.

A copy does not follow its original: when Ada changes her email address, her old orders keep the old one. Where that is wrong, reference the customer instead, but never with @DBRef, which Amazon DocumentDB does not support.

Connecting to Amazon DocumentDBtrap#

One setting holds the connection string, and one names the certificate for Transport Layer Security (TLS). Boot 4 renamed both:

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb://sample-user:password@sample-cluster.node.us-east-1.docdb.amazonaws.com:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&retryWrites=false
      ssl:
        bundle: docdb
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        docdb:
          truststore:
            certificate: file:/etc/billing/global-bundle.pem
spring:
  mongodb:
    uri: mongodb://sample-user:password@sample-cluster.node.us-east-1.docdb.amazonaws.com:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&retryWrites=false
    ssl:
      bundle: docdb
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        docdb:
          truststore:
            certificate: file:/etc/billing/global-bundle.pem
Reading the code
retryWrites=false

The driver sends every write as a retryable write. As of October 2026, Amazon DocumentDB rejects that before engine version 8.0.2, and on elastic clusters: Retryable writes are not supported. From 8.0.2, released on 28 September 2026, you may remove the parameter.

bundle: docdb

Switches TLS on, with the certificates of the bundle below. AWS's strings for other languages carry tlsCAFile; in a local run, the Java driver took no notice of it.

certificate: file:/etc/billing/global-bundle.pem

The certificate authority (CA) file that AWS publishes. Without it: PKIX path building failed. A trust store is the other route.

Two parameters that change behaviourtrap#

To a driver, a cluster is a replica set named rs0: one primary instance takes every write, and replicas serve reads.

Gotcha

readPreference=secondaryPreferred gives up reading your own write. It sends reads to the cluster's replicas, which AWS describes as eventually consistent:

Order saved = orders.save(order);                      // goes to the primary instance
Optional<Order> again = orders.findById(saved.id());   // may go to a replica

So findById can miss the order. Where a read must see the write, read from the primary: leave the parameter out.

Gotcha

Through an SSH tunnel, leave replicaSet=rs0 out. AWS states that connecting in replica set mode through a tunnel results in an error. So the string that works inside AWS fails from your laptop.

What Amazon DocumentDB does not dotrap#

Amazon DocumentDB runs only inside a virtual private cloud (VPC) at AWS, and cannot run on your laptop. So this book develops against a MongoDB container. That is this book's choice, not AWS guidance: AWS's guide is silent on it.

Gotcha

A MongoDB container accepts code that Amazon DocumentDB rejects. DocumentDB emulates the MongoDB API on its own engine, and lacks some features. AWS lists these as unsupported on every engine version, as of October 2026:

AWS lists as unsupportedA Spring Data service reaches it throughInstead
DBRefs@DBRefuse @DocumentReference, or a field that holds the id
$wherean @Query string that uses $whereuse the query operators, such as $gt, $in and $elemMatch
Hashed Index, Wildcard index@HashIndexed, @WildcardIndexeduse a single-field or a compound index
2d Index@GeoSpatialIndexed, with its default typeask for a 2dsphere index, which AWS lists as supported
Capped Collections, cursor.tailable()a capped collection, a tailable cursorAWS names no replacement

One difference is silent: Amazon DocumentDB guarantees no implicit order of results. Name the order in every query that returns a list:

List<Order> findByStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc(OrderStatus status);

OrderByPlacedAtDesc sends a sort with the filter. More differences lists the rest.

Transactionstrap#

PredictA transactional method that saves, then throws#
What does this print?
// The application declares no transaction manager, and the collection is empty.
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void place(Order order) {
        orders.save(order);
        throw new IllegalStateException("payment failed");
    }
}

// in the caller
try {
    service.place(order);
} catch (IllegalStateException e) { }
System.out.println(orders.count());
Show the answer
1

@Transactional does nothing for MongoDB until you declare a MongoTransactionManager. Spring Data's reference says that without one, “transaction support is DISABLED”. Boot 4.1 creates none, so no transaction started and the saved order stayed.

Declare the bean, as below. With it, the same run printed 0.

In .NET the transaction is explicit, so there is nothing to forget. In Spring, declare the manager once:

MongoDB .NET driver
// the session goes to every call
using IClientSessionHandle session = await client.StartSessionAsync();
session.StartTransaction();

await orders.InsertOneAsync(session, order);

await session.CommitTransactionAsync();
Spring Data MongoDB
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.MongoDatabaseFactory;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.MongoTransactionManager;

@Configuration
public class MongoConfig {

    @Bean
    MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(
            MongoDatabaseFactory factory) {
        return new MongoTransactionManager(factory);
    }
}

MongoTransactionManager is an ordinary Spring transaction manager, so the rollback rule and the proxy trap of Transactions apply. In the run it needed a replica set.

Gotcha

One point could not be tested. Spring's transaction manager opens a causally consistent session, and AWS states that Amazon DocumentDB does not support causal consistency. Test a @Transactional method on your cluster first, and read the limits AWS documents.

Indexestrap#

Gotcha

@Indexed(unique = true) enforces nothing by default. Spring Data creates no index unless auto index creation is switched on, and it is off. In the run, two invoices for one order were both saved:

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.index.Indexed;

@Document("invoices")
public record Invoice(@Id String id,
                      @Indexed(unique = true) String orderId,
                      Money total, LocalDate issuedOn) { }

invoices.save(new Invoice(null, "o-1", total, today));
invoices.save(new Invoice(null, "o-1", total, today));
System.out.println(invoices.count());        // prints 2

Nothing rejected the second save. Switch index creation on; the setting has the same name on Boot 3 and Boot 4:

spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      auto-index-creation: true

With auto-index-creation on, the second save threw a DuplicateKeyException. On Amazon DocumentDB an index build blocks its collection by default, so build an index on a large collection outside the application.

Testing without a clustertwist#

@DataMongoTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:8.0");

    @Autowired OrderRepository orders;

    @BeforeEach
    void empty() {
        orders.deleteAll();
    }

    @Test
    void findsByProduct() {
        orders.save(anOrder("A-1"));      // anOrder builds an Order with that product
        assertThat(orders.findByLinesProductId("A-1")).hasSize(1);
    }
}
Reading the code
@DataMongoTest

The test slice for document data. Unlike @DataJpaTest, it rolls nothing back: in the run, the next test still saw this one's order. So each test starts by emptying the collection.

static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:8.0");

Pin the MongoDB version your cluster is compatible with. To test a transaction, add .withReplicaSet(): in the run, the plain container refused one.

A passing test proves less than it seems, because the container accepts features Amazon DocumentDB rejects. Test against a real cluster before a release.

Referencing a document instead of embedding it#

A customer lives without any one order. To store customers once, give them a collection of their own, and let the order hold a reference:

import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.DocumentReference;

@Document("customers")
public record Customer(@Id String id, String name, String email) { }

@Document("orders")
public record Order(@Id String id,
                    @DocumentReference Customer customer,
                    List<OrderLine> lines) { }

@DocumentReference stores only the customer's id in the order. Reading orders in the run then cost one more query for each order, to load its customer: the N+1 problem again. Nothing cascades: you save the customer yourself.

Gotcha

Do not use @DBRef on Amazon DocumentDB. It is Spring Data's other way to reference, and stores a value of the DBRef type. AWS lists that type as not supported on any engine version, as of October 2026.

What the stored document holds: types, names and _class#

A stored document is in BSON: MongoDB's format, with types that JSON lacks, such as ObjectId, Date and Decimal128. Each row below is what a run on 3 October 2026 stored, with Spring Data MongoDB 5.1.1 and the MongoDB .NET driver 3.12.0, both on their defaults:

MemberSpring Data MongoDB storedThe .NET driver stored
the id, a string"_id": an ObjectId"_id": an ObjectId, with [BsonRepresentation]
status, an enum"status": "NEW""Status": 0
placedAt"placedAt": a date, from an Instant"PlacedAt": a date, from a DateTime
amounta Decimal128, from a BigDecimala Decimal128, from a decimal
a field's nameas the Java field: customeras the C# property: Customer
the id of a nested object"_id""_id"
the type"_class": "com.acme.billing.Order"nothing

Two services that share a collection must therefore agree on names and on enums. These attributes and annotations do the agreeing:

MongoDB .NET driver
[BsonIgnoreExtraElements]
public class Product
{
    [BsonId]
    public string Id { get; set; } = "";

    [BsonElement("display_name")]
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";

    [BsonIgnore]
    public string Label { get; set; } = "";
}
Spring Data MongoDB
@Document("products")
@TypeAlias("product")
public class Product {

    @Id
    private String id;

    @Field("display_name")
    private String name;

    @Transient
    private String label;
}
Reading the code
[BsonIgnoreExtraElements]

Lets the .NET class read a document that holds fields it has no property for, such as _class. Without it, the driver threw a FormatException in the run.

@TypeAlias("product")

Stores product in _class, not the class name. So renaming or moving the class does not change what is stored.

@Field("display_name")

Stores the field under another name, as [BsonElement] does.

@Transient

Leaves the field out of the document, as [BsonIgnore] does. It comes from org.springframework.data.annotation.

Gotcha

A LocalDate is stored through the machine's time zone. On a machine set to British summer time, the run stored 3 October 2026 as 2026-10-02T23:00:00Z. It read back correctly on the same machine. Spring Data's reference recommends the driver's own java.time codecs, which use UTC.

Note

Boot 4 sets no representation for a BigDecimal. In the run the driver stored it as a Decimal128, which AWS lists as a supported type. To state the choice, set spring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimal to decimal128.

AWS's Java route: a trust store made with keytool#

AWS's own instructions for Java do not use a PEM file directly. They split global-bundle.pem into its certificates and import each into a Java trust store, because keytool imports one certificate at a time:

curl -sS "https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem" > global-bundle.pem
split -p "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" global-bundle.pem rds-ca-

for CERT in rds-ca-*; do
  keytool -import -file "$CERT" -alias "$CERT" -storepass changeit \
          -keystore rds-truststore.jks -noprompt
done
Reading the code
split -p "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" global-bundle.pem rds-ca-

Writes one file for each certificate. This is the macOS form; AWS's Linux script uses awk.

keytool -import -file "$CERT" -alias "$CERT" -storepass changeit \

keytool comes with the Java Development Kit (JDK). Each certificate needs an alias of its own; AWS's script takes it from the certificate's subject.

Then point the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) at the trust store, or name it in an SSL bundle of the jks kind:

java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=rds-truststore.jks \
     -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit -jar billing.jar

Both routes, javax.net.ssl.trustStore and the jks bundle, connected in a local run against a MongoDB container that accepts only TLS. So did the PEM bundle of the connection section, with a file that held two certificates.

Note

Through an SSH tunnel the host name is localhost, which does not match the cluster's certificate. AWS's shell command adds --sslAllowInvalidHostnames for that. The Java driver's parameter is tlsAllowInvalidHostnames.

More differences: behaviour, engine 5.0 and elastic clusters#

Some features are supported on Amazon DocumentDB and behave differently. AWS states these, as of October 2026:

On Amazon DocumentDBWhat it means for your code
$regexuses an index only with hint(), and best for a prefix without options
allowDiskUsenot supported for find, only as part of an aggregation
cursor.noCursorTimeout()not supported, so leave Query.noCursorTimeout() off
The admin and local databasesnot supported
Write concernthe values you send are ignored; it always writes with majority
Document sizeat most 16 MiB, which is the ceiling for what an order can embed

This chapter describes engine version 8.0 on an instance-based cluster. AWS's table of features by engine version shows what the other two lack:

FeatureEngine 5.0Engine 8.0Elastic clusters
ACID transactionsYesYesNo
Retryable writesNoYes (8.0.2+)No
Change streamsYesYesNo
CollationNoYesNo
ViewsNoYesNo
Text IndexV1V2No
Partial indexYesYesNo
$facetNoYes (8.0.2+)No
$set, $unset and $replaceWith stagesNoYesNo
GridFSYesYesNo

An elastic cluster is sharded, and uses a wire protocol compatible with MongoDB 5.0. AWS does not offer elastic clusters on engine version 8.0. So on an elastic cluster @Transactional has nothing to work with, and retryable writes stay off:

mongodb://sample-user:password@sample-cluster.node.us-east-1.docdb.amazonaws.com:27017/shop?retryWrites=false

The parameter retryWrites=false is required there, and on every engine version before 8.0.2.

Note

Spring Data MongoDB 5.1 states that it is tested against MongoDB 6 to 8. Engine version 8.0 is the only one in that range. That is this book's reading of two sources, not a promise by either vendor.

Transactions on Amazon DocumentDB: the documented limits#

AWS documents these limits for a transaction, as of October 2026. None could be reproduced on a MongoDB container, so none was run:

LimitWhat AWS states
Engine versiontransactions need engine version 4.0 or later
Elastic clustersACID transactions are not supported
New collectionsa transaction cannot create a collection, or query one that does not exist
Durationa transaction has a one minute execution limit
Sizethe transaction log must be smaller than 32 MB
Cursorscursors within a transaction are not supported
Causal consistencynot supported; AWS's own examples switch it off in the session

The collection limit meets a Spring habit: the first save creates a collection that does not exist. Inside a transaction on Amazon DocumentDB it cannot, so create the collection first:

// once, outside any transaction: for example when the application starts
if (!template.collectionExists(Order.class)) {
    template.createCollection(Order.class);
}

collectionExists and createCollection are methods of MongoTemplate. A transaction that runs longer than one minute is aborted, and AWS quotes the error the next command receives: Given transaction number 0 does not match any in-progress transactions.

Check yourself
1
Invoice.orderId carries @Indexed(unique = true), yet two invoices for one order are both saved. Why?
Spring Data creates no index by default, so the annotation alone enforces nothing. Set spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation to true, or create the index yourself.
2
An expert asksYour tests pass against a MongoDB container. Why can the same code still fail on Amazon DocumentDB?
Amazon DocumentDB emulates the MongoDB API on its own engine, and lacks some features, such as DBRefs and $where. Before engine version 8.0.2 it also rejects retryable writes, which the driver sends by default. A container accepts all of them.

SettingBoot 4Boot 3
Connection stringspring.mongodb.urispring.data.mongodb.uri
Database namespring.mongodb.databasespring.data.mongodb.database
SSL bundlespring.mongodb.ssl.bundlespring.data.mongodb.ssl.bundle
Auto index creationspring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creationspring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation
BigDecimal representationspring.data.mongodb.representation.big-decimalno such setting
@DataMongoTest, the packageorg.springframework.boot.data.mongodb.test.autoconfigureorg.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.data.mongo
MongoDBContainer, the packageorg.testcontainers.mongodborg.testcontainers.containers

Security#

Part P9 · ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 44· 7 min read

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters that every request passes through before it reaches your controllers. The filters work out who is calling, and store the answer as an Authentication. Authorisation rules then decide what that caller may do.

KindC#JavaNote
twistClaimsPrincipalAuthentication / Principalthe signed-in user; its authorities play the part of claims Why
twistUser.Identity.Nameauthentication.getName()the principal's name, such as the JWT subject Why
twistAddAuthenticationSecurityFilterChain beanone bean declares how requests are authenticated Why
twistAddAuthorizationauthorizeHttpRequests(...)the URL rules, matched in order inside the same bean Why
twist[AllowAnonymous]permitAll() in the chainusually a path rule in the chain, not an annotation Why
twistCookie authenticationformLogin() + sessionform login backed by an HTTP session Why
twistJwtBeareroauth2ResourceServer().jwt()validates bearer JWTs; set the issuer in application.yml Why
trapURL rules in any orderspecific rules first, anyRequest() lastrules are checked in order, and the first one that matches decides Why
trapAntiforgery tokenCSRF protection, on by defaulton by default: a POST without the token gets a 403 Why
twist[Authorize]@PreAuthorize, or a chain rule@PreAuthorize on methods, or a URL rule in the chain Why
twist[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix for you Why
twistPolicy-based authorisationSpEL in @PreAuthorize, or an AuthorizationManagerwrite the rule as an expression, or as a small bean Why
trapno equivalent@EnableMethodSecuritywithout it, every @PreAuthorize is silently ignored Why
trapUser.IsInRole("Admin")hasRole('ADMIN'), which needs ROLE_ADMINa JWT's roles claim gives no authorities until a converter maps it Why
trapno equivalenta call through another beana call from inside the same class skips the @PreAuthorize check Why
twistUser.FindFirst("sub")@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwta controller parameter receives the caller's validated token Why
twistIdentityUserUserDetailsthe user record Spring Security loads to check a password Why
twistUserManagerUserDetailsServiceloads users by name; account management is yours to build Why
twistData protectionno direct equivalentno built-in key ring; use a KMS or Spring Vault Why
twiststring? in a signature@Nullable from JSpecifySpring Framework 7 says in its own API where null is possible Why

Concept mappingtwist#

Callers prove who they are with a token from an identity provider, using OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC), as in .NET. The token is a JSON Web Token (JWT): a signed piece of JSON that names the user and lists what they may do.

C#
// ClaimsPrincipal: the signed-in user and their claims
string? name = User.Identity?.Name;
bool admin = User.IsInRole("Admin");

builder.Services.AddAuthorization(o =>
    o.AddPolicy("ReadsOrders",
        p => p.RequireClaim("scope", "orders")));
Java 25
// Authentication: the signed-in user and their authorities
Authentication auth =
        SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
String name = auth.getName();
boolean admin = auth.getAuthorities()
        .contains(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN"));

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders')")  // a policy
public Order get(long id) { ... }
Reading the code
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

Where Spring Security keeps the caller of the request being handled.

auth.getName();

The caller's name; for a JWT, its subject.

.contains(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN"));

An authority is a plain string, such as ROLE_ADMIN. A role is simply an authority whose name starts with ROLE_.

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders')")

A rule written as an expression on the method, where ASP.NET Core would use a named policy. A JWT's scopes become authorities with the prefix SCOPE_, so the orders scope is SCOPE_orders.

The filter chaintwist#

You declare one bean of type SecurityFilterChain. You configure it through a domain-specific language (DSL): a chain of method calls on HttpSecurity, each taking a lambda that sets up one part.

C#
builder.Services.AddAuthentication()
    .AddJwtBearer();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers().RequireAuthorization();
Java 25
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http)
            throws Exception {
        return http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**")
                    .hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o ->
                o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            // stateless API only
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(
                SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .build();
    }
}
Reading the code
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth

The URL rules, like AddAuthorization and RequireAuthorization together.

.requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()

Anyone may call the health check, like [AllowAnonymous].

.hasRole("ADMIN")

Paths under /api/admin need the authority ROLE_ADMIN.

.anyRequest().authenticated())

Every other request needs a signed-in caller of any kind.

o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))

Accepts JWT bearer tokens, like AddJwtBearer. withDefaults() takes its settings from application.yml.

.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())

Switches off protection against cross-site request forgery (CSRF). That is safe here only because the API uses tokens, not cookies.

SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))

Never creates an HTTP session: every request carries its own token.

Where the tokens come fromtwist#

One setting tells Spring where the tokens come from. Spring then fetches the provider's signing keys, and checks each token's signature, issuer and expiry:

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://login.acme.example/realms/shop
Reading the code
issuer-uri: https://login.acme.example/realms/shop

The identity provider's address, like Authority in the JwtBearer options.

Two chain traps: rule order and CSRFtrap#

Two lines of the filter chain hold a trap each:

http
    .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
        .anyRequest().authenticated())
    .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
Reading the code
.anyRequest().authenticated())

The broadest rule, so it comes last.

.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());

Switches off protection against cross-site request forgery (CSRF) for the whole API.

Gotcha

Rules are matched in order and the first match wins. Put anyRequest() last, always. A broad rule placed early silently shadows every rule after it, and the failure mode is an endpoint that is more open than you intended.

Gotcha

CSRF protection is on by default, including for POST requests to a JSON API. The attack it stops is another site making the user's browser send a request with the user's cookies. If your first POST returns 403 with no useful message, this is why. Disable it only for an API that browsers do not call with cookies; keep it for anything cookie-based.

Method-level authorisationtwist#

A rule that depends on the method's arguments goes on the method:

C#
[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
public async Task Delete(int id) { ... }

[Authorize(Policy = "OwnsOrder")]
public async Task<Order> Get(int id) { ... }
Java 25
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void delete(long id) { ... }

@PreAuthorize("@orderGuard.owns(#id, authentication)")
public Order get(long id) { ... }
Reading the code
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")

Checked before the method runs, like [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]. If it fails, Spring refuses the call, with 403 Forbidden for a signed-in caller.

@PreAuthorize("@orderGuard.owns(#id, authentication)")

The rule calls a bean. @orderGuard is the bean named orderGuard, #id is the method's id parameter, and authentication is the caller. This is the Spring form of a custom policy.

The guard is an ordinary bean, so it can use the repository:

@Component
class OrderGuard {

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    OrderGuard(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    boolean owns(long orderId, Authentication caller) {
        return orders.findById(orderId)
                .map(order -> order.getCustomerId().equals(caller.getName()))
                .orElse(false);
    }
}
Reading the code
class OrderGuard {

Its bean name, orderGuard, comes from the class name with a lower-case first letter.

.map(order -> order.getCustomerId().equals(caller.getName()))

The caller owns the order when the order's customer id is the caller's name, the token's subject.

These are the expressions you will use most:

ExpressionMeans
hasRole('ADMIN')requires the authority ROLE_ADMIN; the prefix is added for you
hasAuthority('orders:write')requires exactly that authority string, with no prefix added
hasAnyRole('A','B')requires at least one of the roles: ROLE_A or ROLE_B
isAuthenticated()any signed-in user; anonymous requests are refused
permitAll() / denyAll()always allowed, or always refused, whoever is calling
#idrefers to the method parameter named id
authenticationthe current user's Authentication object
@beanName.method(...)call a bean, arbitrary policy logic

Three ways a method rule failstrap#

@PreAuthorize puts a rule on one method. Such annotations do nothing until one configuration class switches them on:

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity      // required, method annotations do nothing without it
public class MethodSecurityConfig { }
Reading the code
@EnableMethodSecurity

Makes Spring wrap beans that carry @PreAuthorize in proxies that check the rule. Without it, the annotations are silently ignored.

PredicthasRole and a JWT with a roles claim#
May this caller call delete?
// The caller's JWT holds:   "scope": "orders",   "roles": ["ADMIN"]
// The application declares no JwtAuthenticationConverter bean.

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void delete(long id) { ... }
Show the answer
No. Spring refuses the call, with 403 Forbidden.

hasRole('ADMIN') checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN. Spring adds the prefix for you in hasRole but not in hasAuthority, and mixing them up produces rules that silently never match. A JWT adds a second trap: by default only its scope claim becomes authorities, as SCOPE_…. A "roles": ["ADMIN"] claim is ignored until you map it.

This bean tells Spring to read the roles claim, and to give each role the ROLE_ prefix so that hasRole('ADMIN') matches:

@Bean
JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthenticationConverter() {
    var roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
    roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");

    var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(roles);
    return converter;
}

setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles") reads authorities from the roles claim instead of scope. It replaces the default, so SCOPE_ authorities are no longer produced. setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_") turns ADMIN into ROLE_ADMIN, the form hasRole checks.

Gotcha

@PreAuthorize is proxy-based, exactly like @Transactional. A call from inside the same class bypasses it entirely, so a security check that relies on self-invocation is no check at all. How Spring actually works explains the mechanism.

The current user#

An endpoint that returns “my orders” needs the caller's id. In ASP.NET Core you read a claim from User. In Spring, a controller parameter receives the token:

C#
public IActionResult Get()
{
    var id = User.FindFirst("sub")?.Value;
    ...
}
Java 25
@GetMapping
public OrderDto get(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    String id = jwt.getSubject();
    ...
}

// or anywhere, without passing it along
var auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
                                .getAuthentication();
Reading the code
@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt

Spring passes in the caller's validated token. getSubject() reads its sub claim, the user's id.

var auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext()

Works in any bean, but hides the dependency. Prefer the parameter in controllers.

Gotcha

SecurityContextHolder keeps the caller in a ThreadLocal, a value that belongs to one thread. So it does not follow work to a thread you start yourself, including tasks you submit to an ExecutorService. Wrap the executor in a DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor to carry the caller across whenever you fan work out.

Passwords#

If the shop stores its own users' passwords, it must hash them. One bean chooses the algorithm:

@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}
Reading the code
PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();

Hashes new passwords with bcrypt, and can still check hashes made with older algorithms.

Note

The delegating encoder stores a prefix such as {bcrypt} in the hash, so you can migrate algorithms without invalidating existing passwords. It is the equivalent of ASP.NET Identity's versioned password hashes, and it is the right default.

Null-safety in the Spring API#

Note

Spring Framework 7 moved its whole API from the Java Specification Request (JSR) 305 annotations to JSpecify Boot 4. If you use a null checker, Spring's own signatures now say exactly where null is possible, generics included. That makes the checker much more useful against Spring than it was on Boot 3. See Nullability.

Here a configuration lookup may return null, and the checker says so. env is Spring's Environment, injected like any bean:

String url = env.getProperty("rates.url");   // declared @Nullable in Spring Framework 7
int length = url.length();                   // a null checker such as NullAway flags this line
Reading the code
String url = env.getProperty("rates.url");

getProperty returns null when the setting is missing, and Spring 7 declares that with JSpecify's @Nullable.

int length = url.length();

Using url without a null check could throw, so a checker such as NullAway reports this line when you build.

Check yourself
1
A method carries @PreAuthorize, yet every caller gets through. Name two possible causes.
No configuration class carries @EnableMethodSecurity, so the annotation is silently ignored. Or the call comes from inside the same class, which bypasses the proxy that checks the rule.
2
An expert asksThe shop's API switches CSRF protection off. Why is that safe there, and not for a site that signs users in with cookies?
The attack is another site making the user's browser send a request with the user's cookies. The shop's API uses tokens, not cookies, so it is safe to switch off. Anything cookie-based must keep the protection.
Next · Part ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot45HTTP clients and resilience6 min

HTTP clients and resilience#

Part P9 · ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 45· 6 min read· Quick reference

Spring's RestClient calls another service over HTTP, as HttpClient does. This chapter also covers interface clients, like Refit, and what takes the place of Polly when the other service fails.

KindC#JavaNote
twisthttpClientFactory.CreateClient("rates")a RestClient bean, built from RestClient.BuilderRestClient is the default client on Boot 3.2 and later, and it blocks Why
twistGetFromJsonAsync<Rate>(url)get().uri(url).retrieve().body(Rate.class)a blocking call, which is exactly right on a virtual thread Why
twistRefit interfacean @HttpExchange interfaceone method per endpoint, and Spring writes the class that makes the calls Why
twistAddRefitClient<IRatesApi>()Boot 3: HttpServiceProxyFactory. Boot 4: @ImportHttpServicesBoot 4 registers the client bean; on Boot 3 you build it in a @Bean method Why
twistConfigureHttpClient(c => c.BaseAddress = ...)spring.http.serviceclient.<group>.base-urlon Boot 4, the address of an @ImportHttpServices group is a setting Why
twistPolly's AddRetryBoot 3: @Retry, from Resilience4j. Boot 4: @RetryableSpring Framework 7 has retry in its core, so Boot 4 needs no extra library Why
twista Polly bulkheadBoot 3: @Bulkhead. Boot 4: @ConcurrencyLimit(10)caps how many calls run at once; virtual threads have no pool that limits them Why
twistPolly's AddCircuitBreaker@CircuitBreaker, from Resilience4jcore has no circuit breaker and no rate limiter, on Boot 3 or on Boot 4 Why
trapMaxRetryAttempts = 3@Retryable(maxRetries = 3)Boot 4 counts only the retries, so 3 means four calls; Boot 3's maxAttempts counted the first Why
trapa pipeline you call yourself@Retryable, which works through a proxya call from inside the same class skips the proxy, so nothing is retried Why
trapa client with no timeout setsetConnectTimeout(...) and setReadTimeout(...)the defaults are effectively infinite, so a hung service holds the connection Why
twistEnsureSuccessStatusCode()retrieve()a 4xx or 5xx reply becomes an exception; onStatus swaps in your own Why
newno equivalentrestTemplate.getForObject(...)the original client, in maintenance mode: write RestClient in new code Why

The client optionstwist#

Spring offers several clients for an HTTP call:

ClientStyleUse when
RestClientfluent, blockingthe default on Boot 3.2+
WebClientfluent, reactiveyou are in WebFlux, or need streaming
@HttpExchange interfacedeclarativeyou want Refit-style typed clients
RestTemplatefluent, blockinglegacy; see below
java.net.http.HttpClientJDK built-inno Spring dependency wanted

The last row is the client built into the Java Development Kit (JDK). Here is the everyday call, in both frameworks:

C#
var client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient("rates");
var rate = await client
    .GetFromJsonAsync<Rate>($"/rates/{pair}");
Java 25
Rate rate = restClient.get()
        .uri("/rates/{pair}", pair)
        .retrieve()
        .body(Rate.class);
Reading the code
.uri("/rates/{pair}", pair)

A URI template: {pair} is filled in, and escaped, from the next argument. The base address was set when the RestClient was built.

.retrieve()

Sends the request. A 4xx or 5xx response becomes an exception, like EnsureSuccessStatusCode.

.body(Rate.class);

Reads the JSON body into a Rate, here a record, record Rate(String pair, double value).

Note

That call blocks, and on a virtual thread that is exactly right. You no longer need WebClient to scale: reactive types are for streaming and backpressure, not for avoiding thread starvation. See Threads are cheap now.

Declarative clientstwist#

Refit
public interface IRatesApi
{
    [Get("/rates/{pair}")]
    Task<Rate> GetRate(string pair);

    [Post("/quotes")]
    Task<Quote> CreateQuote([Body] QuoteRequest req);
}

builder.Services
    .AddRefitClient<IRatesApi>()
    .ConfigureHttpClient(c =>
        c.BaseAddress = new Uri(url));
Spring HTTP interfaces
public interface RatesApi {

    @GetExchange("/rates/{pair}")
    Rate getRate(@PathVariable String pair);

    @PostExchange("/quotes")
    Quote createQuote(@RequestBody QuoteRequest request);
}
Reading the code
@GetExchange("/rates/{pair}")

This method sends a GET to that path, like Refit's [Get]. The same @PathVariable and @RequestBody annotations as in a controller say where each argument goes.

Quote createQuote(@RequestBody QuoteRequest request);

Sends the QuoteRequest as the JSON body, and reads the reply into a Quote.

Boot 4 added auto-configuration for @HttpExchange interfaces. On Boot 3 you build the client yourself:

// Boot 3: build the proxy factory by hand
@Configuration
class ClientConfig {

    @Bean
    RatesApi ratesApi(RestClient.Builder builder,
                      @Value("${rates.url}") String url) {
        RestClient client = builder.baseUrl(url).build();
        var adapter = RestClientAdapter.create(client);
        var factory = HttpServiceProxyFactory
                .builderFor(adapter).build();
        return factory.createClient(RatesApi.class);
    }
}
// Boot 4: declare the group; Spring registers the client bean
@Configuration
@ImportHttpServices(group = "rates", types = RatesApi.class)
class ClientConfig { }

// configured in application.yml under the group name,
// then injected like any other bean
Reading the code
return factory.createClient(RatesApi.class);

On Boot 3, HttpServiceProxyFactory creates a proxy: an object that implements RatesApi by turning each method call into an HTTP request through the RestClient.

@ImportHttpServices(group = "rates", types = RatesApi.class)

On Boot 4, one annotation does the same, and puts the interface in a group called rates whose settings live in application.yml.

Boot 4: the settings of a service group#

On Boot 4, the group's settings sit under its name:

spring:
  http:
    serviceclient:
      rates:
        base-url: https://rates.example.com
Reading the code
base-url: https://rates.example.com

The address every RatesApi call starts from, like BaseAddress in .NET.

Resilience: the Polly answertwist#

C# refresherPolly: retry, circuit breaker and timeout as a pipelineC# 5

Polly composes resilience strategies into one pipeline and runs your call through it.

var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
    .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions { MaxRetryAttempts = 3 })
    .AddCircuitBreaker(new CircuitBreakerStrategyOptions())
    .AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))
    .Build();

var rate = await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(async ct => await FetchAsync(pair, ct));

Spring Framework 7 added retry support to its core, so on Boot 4 @Retryable needs no separate library:

// Boot 3: Resilience4j, added as a dependency
@Service
class RatesClient {

    @Retry(name = "rates", fallbackMethod = "cached")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "rates", fallbackMethod = "cached")
    @Bulkhead(name = "rates")
    public Rate fetch(String pair) {
        return restClient.get()
                .uri("/rates/{p}", pair)
                .retrieve().body(Rate.class);
    }

    private Rate cached(String pair, Throwable t) {
        return cache.get(pair);
    }
}
// Boot 4: @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit are in
// Spring Framework core; no extra dependency
@EnableResilientMethods
@Configuration
class ResilienceConfig { }

@Service
class RatesClient {

    // core defaults: 3 retries, 1s delay, retries any exception
    @Retryable(includes = RatesUnavailableException.class,
               maxRetries = 4, delay = 200, multiplier = 2,
               jitter = 20, maxDelay = 2000)
    @ConcurrencyLimit(10)
    public Rate fetch(String pair) {
        return restClient.get()
                .uri("/rates/{p}", pair)
                .retrieve().body(Rate.class);
    }
}
Reading the code
@Retry(name = "rates", fallbackMethod = "cached")

Boot 3, with Resilience4j: the settings for the rates policy live in application.yml, and cached is called once every attempt has failed.

@Retryable(includes = RatesUnavailableException.class,

Boot 4, in core: retry only when this exception is thrown, at most 4 more times. The first wait is 200 ms and each later wait doubles, give or take 20 ms, but never exceeds 2 seconds.

@ConcurrencyLimit(10)

At most 10 calls run at once; the rest wait. This plays the part of a bulkhead, and matters with virtual threads, which have no pool to limit them.

Here is where each Polly strategy lands on each line:

PollyBoot 3 (Resilience4j)Boot 4 (Spring Framework core)
Retry@Retry@Retryable
Bulkhead@Bulkhead@ConcurrencyLimit
Circuit breaker@CircuitBreakernot in core; keep Resilience4j
Rate limiter@RateLimiternot in core; keep Resilience4j
Timeout@TimeLimiter@Retryable(timeout = ...) caps the whole retry; set a request timeout for each call
FallbackfallbackMethodnot in core; catch the exception once the retries are spent
ProgrammaticRetryRegistryRetryTemplate with RetryPolicy.builder()

Retries: the count, the proxy and what core leaves out#

On Boot 4, the annotation needs no attributes:

@Retryable
public Rate fetch(String pair) {
    return restClient.get().uri("/rates/{p}", pair).retrieve().body(Rate.class);
}
Reading the code
@Retryable

The core defaults apply: 3 retries, 1 second apart, on any exception.

Gotcha

The attribute is maxRetries, not maxAttempts. Spring Retry, the Boot 3 add-on, uses maxAttempts and counts the first call. Framework 7's core annotation uses maxRetries and counts only the retries. So the default of 3 means four calls in total, one second apart, retrying on any exception. Pasting a Boot 3 snippet into a Boot 4 codebase fails to compile, which is the good outcome. Carrying the wrong idea of the count is the bad one.

Note

Core covers retry and concurrency limiting only. It has no circuit breaker and no rate limiter, so Resilience4j remains the answer for those on both versions. @Retryable's timeout limits the whole sequence of attempts, not one call. What the core additions buy is one less dependency for the two cases most services need.

@Retryable also works on reactive methods, adding a retry to the returned Mono or Flux. Every failed attempt publishes a MethodRetryEvent, which you can listen for to log retries.

Gotcha

@Retryable, like @Transactional and @PreAuthorize, works through a proxy; see How Spring actually works. So self-invocation does not retry. And be careful retrying operations that are not idempotent: a POST that timed out may well have succeeded.

Timeoutstrap#

Gotcha

Set timeouts explicitly. The defaults are effectively infinite. A hung downstream service will otherwise hold a connection until the socket dies. This is true of RestClient, RestTemplate and the JDK client alike.

For one client, set the timeouts on its request factory:

@Bean
RestClient ratesClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                       @Value("${rates.url}") String url) {
    var factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
    factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
    factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
    return builder.baseUrl(url).requestFactory(factory).build();
}
Reading the code
factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));

Give up if the connection is not open within 2 seconds.

factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5));

Give up if the reply does not arrive within 5 seconds. The call then fails with a ResourceAccessException, caused by a SocketTimeoutException.

On Boot 4, two settings apply the same limits to every client Boot builds:

spring:
  http:
    clients:
      connect-timeout: 2s
      read-timeout: 5s
Reading the code
read-timeout: 5s

Applies to whichever HTTP library Boot finds, trying Apache HttpClient, then Jetty, then Reactor Netty, then the JDK's own clients.

Error handling#

By default, a 4xx or 5xx response becomes a Spring exception. To turn them into your own exceptions instead, handle each status family:

Rate rate = restClient.get()
        .uri("/rates/{p}", pair)
        .retrieve()
        .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError,
                  (req, res) -> { throw new UnknownPairException(pair); })
        .onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError,
                  (req, res) -> { throw new RatesUnavailableException(); })
        .body(Rate.class);
Reading the code
.onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError,

For any 4xx reply, run this handler instead of the default. Here it throws the shop's own UnknownPairException.

(req, res) -> { throw new RatesUnavailableException(); })

For any 5xx reply, throw the exception that @Retryable above retries on.

Without any handler, these are the defaults:

SituationRestClient default
4xxthrows HttpClientErrorException
5xxthrows HttpServerErrorException
Want the status, not an exceptionuse .exchange(...) instead of .retrieve()

Each exception has a subclass per status, such as HttpClientErrorException.NotFound for a 404, so you can catch exactly the case you expect.

RestTemplate#

LegacyRestTemplate

The original Spring HTTP client, and still in most existing codebases. It is in maintenance mode: not deprecated, but getting no new features, and the documentation steers you to RestClient, which wraps the same infrastructure with a better API.

Rate rate = restTemplate.getForObject(
        "/rates/{p}", Rate.class, pair);
Reading the code
restTemplate.getForObject(

One method per verb and result: a GET, with the body read into a Rate. The URI template works as in RestClient.

Migration is mostly mechanical, and a RestClient can be built from an existing RestTemplate's configuration with RestClient.create(restTemplate).

Check yourself
1
What takes the place of Polly on Boot 3, and what on Boot 4?
Boot 3 uses the Resilience4j library. On Boot 4, @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit are in Spring Framework itself. For a circuit breaker or a rate limiter you still add Resilience4j, on both.

Quick reference#

SettingUse it to
spring.http.clients.connect-timeoutlimit the wait for a connection, for every client
spring.http.clients.read-timeoutlimit the wait for a reply, for every client
spring.http.serviceclient.<group>.base-urlset the address for an @ImportHttpServices group

Messaging and WebSockets#

Part P9 · ASP.NET Core to Spring Boot · Chapter 46· 6 min read

Messaging between services has the shape you know from MassTransit or the raw client libraries: a Template class sends, and a method with a listener annotation receives. Push to the browser is different: Spring has no single SignalR equivalent.

KindC#JavaNote
twistProduceAsync (Confluent.Kafka)kafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, value)records with the same key go to one partition, so they stay in order Why
twistConsume loopa @KafkaListener methodSpring calls the method for each record, so there is no loop to write Why
trapan exception in the consume loopa listener method that throwsredelivered nine more times, then logged and skipped, unless you add a dead-letter topic Why
trapa publish inside a database transactionkafkaTemplate.send inside @Transactionala rollback does not take the message back; use a transactional outbox, as in .NET Why
twist_bus.Publish(event)rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(exchange, routingKey, event)MassTransit chooses the exchange for you; with Spring AMQP you name it Why
twistIConsumer<T> (MassTransit)a @RabbitListener methodSpring calls the method for each message on the queue Why
twistMassTransit sagas and schedulingno equivalentSpring AMQP leaves these to you; Spring Integration, Camel and Axon come nearest Why
newno equivalentjmsClient.destination("orders").send(event)Jakarta Messaging is Java's standard messaging API; JmsClient needs Boot 4 Why
newMapHub<PricesHub>("/prices")a STOMP broker over WebSocket, with @MessageMappingno Java framework bundles what SignalR does, so Spring gives you the pieces Why
twistClients.Group(...).SendAsyncmessagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/...", payload)pushes to every client subscribed to that destination Why
trapa SignalR backplaneenableStompBrokerRelay, to RabbitMQ or ActiveMQenableSimpleBroker is in memory, so it works on one instance only Why
twistTypedResults.ServerSentEventsSseEmitter, or a Flux on WebFluxserver-sent events are less machinery than WebSocket when only the server pushes Why

Kafkatrap#

With Kafka, the producer sends to a topic and the consumer listens on it:

Confluent.Kafka / MassTransit
// producer
await _producer.ProduceAsync("orders",
    new Message<string, string> {
        Key = order.Id, Value = json });

// consumer
_consumer.Subscribe("orders");
while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    var cr = _consumer.Consume(ct);
    Handle(cr.Message.Value);
}
Spring Kafka
// producer
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", order.id(), order);

// consumer
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders",
               groupId = "billing")
public void handle(OrderPlaced order) {
    process(order);
}
Reading the code
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", order.id(), order);

Sends the event to the orders topic, keyed by the order's id. Events with the same key go to the same partition, so one order's events stay in order.

@KafkaListener(topics = "orders",

Spring calls this method for each record on the topic, Kafka's word for a message, and turns the JSON into an OrderPlaced. There is no loop to write.

groupId = "billing")

The consumer group. Each record goes to one listener in the group.

The Kafka settings in application.ymldeep dive

Boot builds the template and the listeners from settings like these:

spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: billing
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      properties:
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.acme.billing.events"
    producer:
      acks: all
Reading the code
auto-offset-reset: earliest

A new consumer group starts from the oldest record still on the topic, rather than only new ones.

spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.acme.billing.events"

The JSON reader only creates classes from this package, so a message cannot make it build an arbitrary type.

acks: all

A send counts as done only when every in-sync replica has the record.

Gotcha

The listener method commits the offset by returning normally. If it throws, Spring's default error handler redelivers the record up to nine more times, with no pause. Then it logs the record at ERROR level and moves on. So an unhandled exception drops the message, leaving only a log line. Configure a DefaultErrorHandler with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer so failures land in a dead-letter topic rather than disappearing.

Ordering, retries and the outbox#

These settings come up once a Kafka consumer meets production traffic:

ConcernSpring Kafka
Orderingguaranteed per partition only; key by aggregate id to keep an entity's events ordered
Concurrencyconcurrency = "3" on @KafkaListener, capped by partition count
Manual acksAckMode.MANUAL plus an Acknowledgment parameter
Retry with backoffDefaultErrorHandler with an ExponentialBackOff
Dead letterDeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, publishes to topic-dlt
Batch consumptionbatch = "true" and a List parameter
TransactionsKafkaTransactionManager, but it does not span Kafka and your database

Here is the dead-letter setup the gotcha above recommends:

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    var toDeadLetter = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);   // failures go to orders-dlt
    return new DefaultErrorHandler(toDeadLetter, new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3));   // 3 retries, 1 s apart
}
Reading the code
var toDeadLetter = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);

Once the retries are spent, publishes the failed record to a topic named after the original with -dlt added, on the same partition. The dead-letter topic therefore needs at least as many partitions as the original.

new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3)

Three retries after the first delivery, one second apart: four deliveries in all.

Gotcha

There is no distributed transaction across Kafka and your database. Publishing inside an @Transactional method that later rolls back still sends the message. The standard fix is the transactional outbox: write the event to a table in the same transaction, and let a separate poller publish it. It is the same problem, and the same solution, as in .NET; Transactions in depth covers it.

RabbitMQ#

RabbitMQ speaks the Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP), and Spring AMQP is its client. The producer publishes to an exchange with a routing key; the consumer listens on a queue:

C#
_bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced(order.Id));

public class Consumer : IConsumer<OrderPlaced>
{
    public Task Consume(
        ConsumeContext<OrderPlaced> ctx) { ... }
}
Java 25
rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(
    "orders.exchange", "order.placed", event);

@RabbitListener(queues = "orders.queue")
public void handle(OrderPlaced event) { ... }
Reading the code
rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(

Converts the event to a message and publishes it to the orders.exchange exchange with the routing key order.placed. MassTransit chooses the exchange for you; here you name it.

@RabbitListener(queues = "orders.queue")

Spring calls this method for each message on the queue, like IConsumer.

The rest is configuration you declare yourself:

ConceptSpring AMQP
Declare topology@Bean Queue / TopicExchange / Binding
SerialisationJacksonJsonMessageConverter, registered as a bean; Jackson2JsonMessageConverter on Boot 3
Retryspring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.retry.*
Dead letterx-dead-letter-exchange argument on the queue
Manual ackAcknowledgeMode.MANUAL plus a Channel parameter
Note

MassTransit and NServiceBus do a great deal that Spring AMQP leaves to you: saga state, scheduling, conventional routing. The nearest Java equivalents are Spring Integration, Apache Camel and Axon, and none of them is a drop-in replacement.

JMS and JmsClient#

Java also has a standard messaging API, Jakarta Messaging (JMS), used with brokers such as ActiveMQ Artemis and IBM MQ. Spring has long wrapped it in JmsTemplate, and Spring Framework 7 adds a fluent JmsClient on top Boot 4:

jmsClient.destination("orders")
        .send(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));

Optional<OrderPlaced> next = jmsClient.destination("orders")
        .withReceiveTimeout(1000)
        .receive(OrderPlaced.class);
Reading the code
jmsClient.destination("orders")

Picks the queue or topic, then describes the operation on it.

.receive(OrderPlaced.class);

Waits up to the timeout for one message, and returns it as an Optional, empty if none arrived. For a steady stream, a method marked @JmsListener works like @KafkaListener.

WebSockets and the SignalR gapnew#

The shop's web page shows live exchange rates, pushed from the server as they change. In ASP.NET Core that is a SignalR hub:

C# refresherSignalR hubs: server push to groups of clientsC# 6
public class PricesHub : Hub
{
    public Task Subscribe(string pair) =>
        Groups.AddToGroupAsync(Context.ConnectionId, pair);
}

app.MapHub<PricesHub>("/prices");
await hub.Clients.Group("GBPUSD").SendAsync("price", price);   // push to one group
SignalR

There is no Java framework that bundles what SignalR does. SignalR gives you a hub abstraction, automatic transport negotiation and fallback, typed clients, reconnection and backplane scale-out in one library. Spring gives you the pieces:

SignalR featureSpring equivalent
Hub@Controller with @MessageMapping, over STOMP
Strongly typed hub clientnone; you send to a destination by name
Transport fallbacknone built in; WebSocket, with SockJS as an optional fallback
GroupsSTOMP destinations, or a broker topic
Backplane for scale-outan external broker: RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ as a STOMP relay
Automatic reconnectclient-side library concern

The nearest thing to a hub is a broker that speaks the Simple Text Oriented Messaging Protocol (STOMP) over WebSocket. Clients subscribe to named destinations, such as /topic/prices, and the server sends to them:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
public class WsConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void registerStompEndpoints(StompEndpointRegistry registry) {
        registry.addEndpoint("/ws").setAllowedOriginPatterns("*");
    }

    @Override
    public void configureMessageBroker(MessageBrokerRegistry registry) {
        registry.enableSimpleBroker("/topic");     // in-memory, single instance
        registry.setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app");
    }
}

@Controller
class PriceController {

    // client sends to /app/subscribe, replies go to /topic/prices
    @MessageMapping("/subscribe")
    @SendTo("/topic/prices")
    public Price onSubscribe(SubscribeRequest req) {
        return prices.current(req.pair());
    }
}

// push from anywhere in the application
messagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/prices", price);
Reading the code
registry.addEndpoint("/ws").setAllowedOriginPatterns("*");

The address browsers open the WebSocket on, like MapHub. Allow only your own front end's origin in production, not *.

registry.enableSimpleBroker("/topic");

A broker inside the application, which delivers anything sent to a /topic/… destination to every client subscribed to it.

@MessageMapping("/subscribe")

Handles messages the client sends to /app/subscribe, like a hub method. prices is a service that returns the latest price.

messagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/prices", price);

messagingTemplate is Spring's SimpMessagingTemplate, injected like any bean. It pushes to every subscriber, like Clients.Group(...).SendAsync.

Gotcha

enableSimpleBroker is an in-memory broker. It works perfectly on one instance and breaks the moment you scale out, because a message published on instance A never reaches a client connected to instance B. For more than one replica you need enableStompBrokerRelay pointing at RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, which is the equivalent of adding a SignalR backplane.

Server-sent events, the simpler option#

If you only need push from server to client, and not both directions, server-sent events are far less machinery than WebSocket, and pass through most load balancers and firewalls. ASP.NET Core 10 has them built in, and Spring MVC, Spring's model-view-controller (MVC) web framework, has SseEmitter:

C#
// ASP.NET Core 10; Prices(ct) is an IAsyncEnumerable<Price>
app.MapGet("/prices", (CancellationToken ct) =>
    TypedResults.ServerSentEvents(Prices(ct),
        eventType: "price"));
Java 25
@GetMapping(value = "/prices",
    produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public SseEmitter stream() {
    var emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);   // no timeout
    executor.submit(() -> {
        try {
            emitter.send(price);
            emitter.complete();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            emitter.completeWithError(e);
        }
    });
    return emitter;
}
Reading the code
var emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);

An open response that the method returns at once and fills in later. 0L means it never times out.

executor.submit(() -> {

The sending happens on another thread, from an executor of virtual threads, while the request thread is free.

emitter.send(price);

Writes one event, data:{"pair":"GBPUSD","value":1.27}, followed by a blank line. send can throw IOException, hence the try.

emitter.complete();

Ends the stream. A real price feed would keep sending instead.

Note

On WebFlux, Spring's reactive web stack, you simply return a Flux<Price> with the same produces. And on virtual threads, an SseEmitter fed from a blocking loop is now a reasonable design where it once would not have been. See Threads are cheap now.

Check yourself
1
A @KafkaListener method throws every time it receives one record. What happens to that record by default?
Spring redelivers it up to nine more times, with no pause, then logs it at ERROR level and moves on. The message is dropped, unless a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer sends it to a dead-letter topic.
