The JVM at runtime: memory, GC and containers#

Part P10 · Ship it · Chapter 52· 6 min read

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is tuned with command-line flags, and needs it more often than the CLR. Two choices matter: the heap's size in a container, and which garbage collector (GC) runs. The defaults are good, so measure with Java Flight Recorder (JFR) before you change one.

KindC#JavaNote
trapGCHeapHardLimit-Xmx / -XX:MaxRAMPercentagecaps the heap only; metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers need 25 to 30 percent more Why
twistGen0/1/2Young / OldG1 is region-based, not strictly generational Why
twistLOHhumongous regions in G1large objects get their own regions, and collect poorly Why
twist"System.GC.Server": true in runtimeconfig.jsonjava -XX:+UseG1GC -jar app.jarthe .NET GC settings are command-line flags on the JVM Why
twistDOTNET_GCHeapCount-XX:ParallelGCThreadshow many threads the collector uses in parallel Why
twistGC.Collect()System.gc()HotSpot runs a full collection; -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns it off Why
trap"System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 70-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70the default is 25, so a 1 GB container gets a 256 MB heap unless you set a share Why
trapa fixed heap size in the image-XX:MaxRAMPercentage, not -Xmx2g-Xmx2g in an image that later runs with a 1 GB limit gets OOMKilled; a percentage adapts Why
trapmemory for loaded classes-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256mmetaspace has no limit by default, so a class-loading leak can consume the container Why
twistServer GCG1 (default)the default, except on very small machines, where Serial is chosen Why
twistWorkstation GCSerialGCa single-threaded collector, for small heaps and tools Why
twistGCSettings.LatencyModechoice of collectorpick ZGC or Shenandoah when pauses matter more than throughput Why
newno equivalent-XX:+UseZGCpauses stay under 1 ms whatever the heap size, where Server GC pauses grow with the heap Why
trapan old start script-XX:+ZGenerationalthe flag no longer exists, so the JVM refuses to start; -XX:+UseZGC is already generational Why
twistdotnet-counters ps, dotnet-gcdumpjcmd -l, jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dumpjcmd inspects a running JVM: its flags, heap, threads and Flight Recorder Why
trapa pool of 500 threads500 platform threads, at about 1 MB of stack eachthe stacks are reserved outside the heap; a virtual thread keeps its stack on the heap Why
twistBenchmarkDotNetJMHcode is interpreted first and compiled once hot, so benchmarks and new instances need warmup Why

The memory modeltrap#

The billing service's container has a memory limit, and the JVM must fit inside it. This start command looks as if it keeps the service under 512 MB:

java -Xmx512m -jar app.jar

It does not. A JVM process uses memory in several regions, and -Xmx512m sets the size of only the first:

RegionLimited byHolds
Heap-Xmx, or -XX:MaxRAMPercentageyour objects: a young generation for new ones, an old one for survivors
Metaspace-XX:MaxMetaspaceSizeclass metadata; unbounded by default
Code cache-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSizemachine code compiled while the program runs
Thread stacks-Xssabout 1 MB for each platform thread
GC overheadthe collector itselfthe bookkeeping the collector needs
Direct and native memory-XX:MaxDirectMemorySizeByteBuffers, Netty buffers and JNI allocations
Gotcha

-Xmx is not a limit on the process. It bounds the heap only. A container killed with OOMKill while heap usage looks fine is almost always out of metaspace, the stacks of platform threads, or direct buffers. Budget roughly 25 to 30 percent above -Xmx for everything else, or use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage and let the JVM do the arithmetic.

GC settings are command-line flagstwist#

C# refresherGC.Collect, generations and GCSettings.LatencyModeC# 1
GC.Collect();                                   // force a full collection: rarely wise
int gen = GC.GetGeneration(order);              // 0, 1 or 2
GCSettings.LatencyMode = GCLatencyMode.SustainedLowLatency;   // avoid blocking gen 2 GCs

In .NET you tune the GC in runtimeconfig.json. On the JVM the same choices are command-line flags. Here the service takes 70% of the container's memory for its heap:

runtimeconfig.json / env
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.GC.Server": true,
    "System.GC.HeapHardLimitPercent": 70
  }
}
JVM flags
java -XX:+UseG1GC \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 \
     -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
     -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -jar app.jar
Reading the code
-XX:+UseG1GC \

G1, the default collector; the flag only makes the choice visible.

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 \

The heap may grow to 70% of the memory the container is given, like HeapHardLimitPercent.

-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \

Caps class metadata, which otherwise has no limit at all.

-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \

On an OutOfMemoryError the process exits, so the orchestrator restarts it, instead of limping on in a broken state.

The differences table at the top of this chapter maps the other .NET GC settings to their JVM counterparts.

Containerstrap#

The JVM has been container-aware since Java 10: it reads the container's CPU and memory limits rather than the host's. But the default heap is only a quarter of the memory limit. This shows it, then takes a deliberate share instead:

# a 1 GB container: the default max heap is ~25% of it, i.e. ~256 MB
docker run -m 1g eclipse-temurin:25 java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize

# take a deliberate share instead
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar
Reading the code
docker run -m 1g eclipse-temurin:25 java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize

Starts a JVM in a container limited to 1 GB and prints its maximum heap: 256 MB, because the default MaxRAMPercentage is 25.

java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar

With 70%, the same container allows a heap of about 718 MB, leaving the rest for metaspace, thread stacks and buffers.

Gotcha

Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage rather than a fixed -Xmx in a container. A hardcoded -Xmx2g in an image that later runs with a 1 GB limit gets OOMKilled; a percentage adapts. And always set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize: metaspace is unbounded by default, and a class-loading leak will consume the container.

These flags are worth setting in every container:

FlagDoes
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70heap as a share of the container limit
-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=70avoid heap resizing churn
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256mbound class metadata
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryErrordie rather than limp; let the orchestrator restart you
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryErrorwrite a dump for analysis
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumpswhere to write it
-Xss512ksmaller platform thread stacks

Choosing a collectornew#

The JVM offers several collectors, each trading pause times against throughput:

CollectorPause timesThroughputUse when
SerialGChighfine for tiny heapssmall containers, CLI tools
ParallelGChigh, but efficienthighestbatch jobs; latency does not matter
G1 (default)~10-200 msvery goodalmost everything
ZGCunder 1 msslightly lowerlarge heaps, latency-critical
Shenandoahunder 1 msslightly loweras ZGC; not in every Java build; generational mode is optional since Java 25

A single flag picks one:

java -XX:+UseG1GC        -jar app.jar    # default; leave it alone
java -XX:+UseZGC         -jar app.jar    # generational by default since Java 23
java -XX:+UseSerialGC    -jar app.jar    # small container, single CPU
Reading the code
java -XX:+UseG1GC -jar app.jar

G1 is chosen anyway, except on a machine with a single CPU or very little memory, where the JVM picks Serial by itself.

java -XX:+UseZGC -jar app.jar

ZGC does almost all its work while your threads keep running. Since Java 24 its generational mode is the only mode.

java -XX:+UseSerialGC -jar app.jar

One GC thread and the least overhead, for tools and tiny containers.

Gotcha

Old start scripts often carry -XX:+ZGenerational. On current versions of the Java Development Kit (JDK), that flag no longer exists, and the JVM refuses to start: “Unrecognized VM option 'ZGenerational'”. Delete it; generational ZGC is what -XX:+UseZGC gives you.

Note

ZGC's pause times are essentially independent of heap size. A 100 GB heap pauses about as long as a 4 GB one, because the work is concurrent. There is no .NET equivalent: even Server GC with background collection has pauses that scale with the heap. If you have a large-heap, latency-sensitive service, this is a genuine reason to prefer the JVM.

Diagnosing#

When a service misbehaves, these commands inspect the running JVM. jcmd comes with the JDK and finds a JVM by its process id:

jcmd -l                              # list JVMs, like dotnet-counters ps
jcmd <pid> VM.flags                  # what flags are actually in effect
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info              # heap usage now
jcmd <pid> Thread.print              # full thread dump
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram        # what is on the heap, by class
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof      # heap dump for Eclipse MAT
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/r.jfr

jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>   # the older way to take a heap dump

java '-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime' -jar app.jar   # GC logging
Reading the code
jcmd <pid> VM.flags

The flags in effect, including the ones the JVM chose for itself, such as the collector.

jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram

Counts objects by class, largest first: the quickest way to see what is filling the heap.

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

Writes every object on the heap to a file, for analysis in a tool such as Eclipse MAT, like dotnet-gcdump.

java '-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime' -jar app.jar

Logs every collection to gc.log, with the time of day and the time since start. The quotes stop shells such as zsh from treating the * as a file pattern.

Each symptom points at a first place to look:

SymptomLook at
Container OOMKilled, heap looks finemetaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers
Long pausesGC logs; consider ZGC
High CPU, low throughputJFR CPU profile, or async-profiler
Memory grows steadilyheap dump, then Eclipse MAT dominator tree
Threads climbingthread dump; a leaked executor
Slow startupAOT cache, CDS, or the auto-configuration report
Gotcha

Thread stacks are the hidden cost of platform threads. Each platform thread reserves around 1 MB. A pool of 500 threads is 500 MB of address space before your application allocates anything. This is one more reason virtual threads matter: their stacks live on the heap and start at a few hundred bytes. See Threads are cheap now.

The JIT and warmup#

Note

The JVM starts by interpreting your code. Then its just-in-time (JIT) compiler compiles the methods that run often: first quickly, with the C1 compiler, then thoroughly, with C2, for the hottest. Peak performance therefore arrives only after thousands of executions. That is why a Java benchmark that does not warm up is worthless, and why the Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH) exists. It is BenchmarkDotNet's counterpart, and handles warmup, forking and dead-code elimination for you.

The practical consequence in production: the first few hundred requests after a deploy are measurably slower. Java 25's ahead-of-time (AOT) method profiling reduces this, by carrying profile data from a training run. If you run a load balancer with aggressive health checks, give a new instance a moment before sending it full traffic.

You can watch the compiler work:

# watch the JIT at work: each line is a method being compiled as it gets hot
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar | head
Reading the code
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar app.jar | head

Prints one line for each method the JIT compiles, so you can see which of your methods turn hot as the service warms up.

Check yourself
1
Your container is OOMKilled but the heap graph looks flat. Where is the memory?
Outside the heap: metaspace, thread stacks or direct buffers. -Xmx bounds the heap only, so budget 25 to 30 percent above it for everything else.
2
Why prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage to a fixed -Xmx in an image?
A hardcoded -Xmx2g in an image later run with a 1 GB limit gets OOMKilled. A percentage adapts to whatever limit the container is given.

Java in 18 minutes#

Part TOURS · Quick tours · Chapter 53· 18 min read

This is the Java language as one listing of commented code, in the order of the book's chapters. Read it from top to bottom to refresh your memory. The link above each stop opens the section that explains it.

What transfers unchanged
// Most of C# carries over: classes, generics, exceptions, lambdas and var.
// C#: public sealed class OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
public final class OrderService {                        // final class: C#'s sealed
    private final OrderRepository repository;            // final field: C#'s readonly

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {    // no primary constructors
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    // C#: public async Task<Order> PlaceAsync(Order order)
    public Order place(Order order) {                    // camelCase, no async, no Task
        if (order.lines().isEmpty())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("An order needs at least one line.");
        repository.save(order);                          // no await: the call simply blocks
        return order;
    }
}
Getting a JDK, and the release train
// The JDK is Java's SDK: the compiler, the runtime and the tools. C#: the .NET SDK.
// Java ships every six months. Run a long-term support release: 21 or 25.
//   sdk list java                   lists every JDK with its exact identifier
//   sdk install java 25.0.4-tem     SDKMAN keeps several JDKs side by side
//   sdk use java 21.0.12+1.1-tem    switches this shell only
//   java -version                   shows which JDK is really in use
One program, start to finish
// A package is a namespace that must match the folder: src/com/acme/orders/App.java.
package com.acme.orders;                         // C#: namespace Acme.Orders;

import java.math.BigDecimal;                     // an import names a type, not a namespace
import java.util.*;                              // or every type in one package
import static java.util.stream.Collectors.*;     // C#: using static
// The tour leaves out its other imports.

public class App {                               // a public class sits in a file with its name
    public static void main(String[] args) {     // C#: static void Main(string[] args)
        System.out.println("hello");             // prints hello
    }
}
// javac -d out src/com/acme/orders/*.java    writes out/com/acme/orders/App.class
// java -cp out com.acme.orders.App           the classpath, then package plus class
// java -jar app.jar                          reads the main class from the JAR, ignores -cp
The classpath is a search list
// The classpath is the ordered list of folders and JARs that Java searches for a class.
// A JAR is a zip of class files. C#: an assembly.
// The first match wins. Two versions of one library do not conflict: the first one
// silently wins, and you get NoSuchMethodError at run time.
Declaration
// C#: public abstract class Gateway
public abstract class Gateway {                  // abstract means what it means in C#
    protected final String url;
    protected Gateway(String url) { this.url = url; }
}

// C#: public static class MoneyMath
// Java has no static classes: write a final class with a private constructor.
// It has no structs and no partial classes either.
public final class MoneyMath {
    private MoneyMath() { }
    public static BigDecimal round(BigDecimal v) { return v.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); }
}
Constructors and chaining
// C#: public class CardGateway : Gateway, IDisposable
// extends names the one superclass. implements lists the interfaces.
public class CardGateway extends Gateway implements AutoCloseable {
    public CardGateway() {
        this("https://pay.example");             // C#: : this(...)
    }

    public CardGateway(String url) {
        // A check before super(...) is legal since Java 25.
        if (url.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no url");
        super(url);                              // C#: : base(url)
    }

    @Override public void close() { }            // AutoCloseable is IDisposable
}
7. Inner classes capture the outer instance
// A C# nested class is always independent. In Java, only a static one is.
public class Outer {
    class Inner { }            // holds a hidden reference to its Outer, and keeps it alive
    static class Nested { }    // independent: make this your default
}
The mapping
// C#: a member with no modifier is private. In Java it is package-private.
public class Account {
    BigDecimal balance;            // every class in the package can read and change it
    private BigDecimal fee;        // what a C# field with no modifier means
    protected BigDecimal limit;    // subclasses, and also the whole package
}
// Java has no internal. Packages do not nest: com.acme.orders.internal cannot see
// the package-private members of com.acme.orders.
Interfaces
// C#: public interface IOrderRepository. Java drops the I prefix.
public interface OrderRepository {
    void save(Order order);
    Optional<Order> findById(long id);

    default boolean exists(long id) {            // a default method, as in C# 8
        return findById(id).isPresent();
    }
}
// Java has no explicit interface implementation, and no events either:
// a list of listeners replaces a C# event.
Sealed types: Java's discriminated unions
// A sealed interface names the only types that may implement it. C# has no equivalent.
// It is not C#'s sealed: that is Java's final.
public sealed interface Payment permits Card, BankTransfer, Voucher { }
public record Card(String last4) implements Payment { }
public record BankTransfer(String iban) implements Payment { }
public record Voucher(String code) implements Payment { }
6. Methods are virtual by default
// Every method is virtual unless you mark it final. C# opts in with virtual.
class Discount {
    Discount() { describe(); }                   // calls a method that can be overridden
    void describe() { }
}
class SeasonalDiscount extends Discount {
    private String season = "winter sale";
    @Override void describe() { System.out.println(season); }
}
// @Override is optional, but always write it: the compiler then checks the signature.

new SeasonalDiscount();    // prints null: the override ran before season was set
Signatures
// C#: string Label(Payment p, string currency = "EUR")
// Java has no optional or named parameters. Write overloads, or use a builder.
String label(Payment p) { return label(p, "EUR"); }
String label(Payment p, String currency) { return p + " in " + currency; }

// No ref and no out: everything is passed by value. Return a record or an Optional.
// No extension methods and no operator overloading, both unlike C#:
// call a static helper or an ordinary method.
Lambdas and method references
// A C# delegate is a functional interface in Java: an interface with one abstract method.
List<String> productIds = List.of("mug", "cup", "pot");
Predicate<String> isMug = id -> id.equals("mug");     // C#: Func<string, bool>, with =>
Function<String, Integer> length = String::length;    // a method reference; C#: a method group
Supplier<List<String>> fresh = ArrayList::new;        // a constructor reference
Consumer<String> print = System.out::println;         // C#: Action<string>
boolean mug = isMug.test("mug");                      // true: call the interface's method by name

// A lambda may use a local variable only if it is never reassigned. C# has no such rule.
int count = 0;
// productIds.forEach(id -> count++);                 // does not compile
var counter = new AtomicInteger();                    // the usual replacement
productIds.forEach(id -> counter.incrementAndGet());
int counted = counter.get();                          // 3
The property gap
// C#: public Money Total { get; set; }
// Java has no properties: write a private field and methods named getX and setX.
public class Invoice {
    public static final int MAX_LINES = 50;      // C#: const, or static readonly
    private Money total;
    public Money getTotal() { return total; }
    public void setTotal(Money total) { this.total = total; }
}
// Jackson and Hibernate find a property by these exact names.
// Get the prefix wrong and the value is silently missing.
Checking values: the compact constructor
// C#: public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
    public Money {                               // a compact constructor: no parameter list
        if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
        amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);   // assigns the parameter
    }                                            // Java then copies each parameter into its field

    public Money(String amount) {                // an extra constructor calls the main one
        this(new BigDecimal(amount), "EUR");
    }
}
The basics
// C#: public record OrderLine(string ProductId, int Quantity, Money UnitPrice);
public record OrderLine(String productId, int quantity, Money unitPrice) {
    // Java has no with expression, so you write the "wither" yourself.
    public OrderLine withQuantity(int q) { return new OrderLine(productId, q, unitPrice); }
}
public record Customer(long id, String name, String email) { }   // the braces are required

var line = new OrderLine("mug", 2, new Money("9.50"));
int quantity = line.quantity();                  // 2: an accessor method with no get prefix
var more = line.withQuantity(3);                 // C#: line with { Quantity = 3 }
boolean sameLine = line.equals(new OrderLine("mug", 2, new Money("9.5")));   // true: by value
System.out.println(line);
// prints OrderLine[productId=mug, quantity=2, unitPrice=Money[amount=9.50, currency=EUR]]
// A record is always a reference type: Java has no record struct.
A record can still change
// A record is only shallowly immutable, as in C#: copy any list it is given.
public record Order(long id, Customer customer, List<OrderLine> lines, OrderStatus status) {
    public Order {
        lines = List.copyOf(lines);              // a copy that nobody can change
    }
}

var ada = new Customer(1, "Ada Doe", "ada@example.com");
var order = new Order(1042, ada, List.of(line), OrderStatus.PAID);
order.lines().add(more);                         // throws UnsupportedOperationException
Type patterns
Payment payment = new Card("4242");
if (payment instanceof Card card) {              // C#: if (payment is Card card)
    System.out.println(card.last4());            // prints 4242
}
// C#'s is not: !(payment instanceof Card card)
Pattern matching in switch
// Payment is sealed, so the compiler knows every kind and no default is needed.
// Add a fourth kind and this stops compiling until you handle it. C# cannot check that.
String describe(Payment p) {
    return switch (p) {                                          // C#: p switch { ... }
        case null -> "not paid yet";                             // without this arm, null throws
        case Card c when c.last4().equals("0000") -> "a test card";   // a guard, as in C#
        case Card(String last4) -> "card ending " + last4;       // a record pattern
        case BankTransfer t -> "transfer from " + t.iban();
        case Voucher _ -> "a voucher";                           // _ is an unnamed variable
    };
}
// Java has no property, list or relational patterns: test those in a when guard.

String described = describe(payment);            // "card ending 4242"
The arrow form
var day = DayOfWeek.FRIDAY;                      // an enum from java.time
String packing = switch (day) {                  // C#: day switch { ... }
    case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "packed on Monday";             // a comma, where C# writes or
    case FRIDAY -> "packed today, delivered next week";
    default -> "packed today";                               // C#: _ =>
};
// A block arm returns its value with yield, which is unrelated to C#'s yield return.
// The old form, case X: with break, falls through when a break is missing.
var
var lines = new ArrayList<OrderLine>();          // var, as in C#: local variables only
var mixed = new ArrayList<>();                   // a trap: this is an ArrayList<Object>
List<OrderLine> declared = new ArrayList<>();    // the diamond <> takes OrderLine from the left
No string interpolation
// C#: $"Order {id} comes to {total:F2} EUR"
// Java has no string interpolation. Join with +, or use formatted.
long id = 1042;
double total = 59.5;
String joined = "Order " + id + " comes to " + total + " EUR";
String formatted = "Order %d comes to %.2f EUR".formatted(id, total);
// "Order 1042 comes to 59.50 EUR", with an English locale

// A text block is C#'s raw string literal, except that it still processes escapes like \n.
String json = """
    {"orderId": %d, "status": "PAID"}
    """.formatted(id);                           // the indentation is stripped
Comparing strings
String typed = "spring".toUpperCase();           // built while the program runs
boolean sameObject = typed == "SPRING";          // false: == compares references, not text
boolean sameText = typed.equals("SPRING");       // true: C#'s == on strings
boolean nullSafe = Objects.equals(typed, null);  // false, and no exception if either is null
Enums with state and behaviour
// C#: enum OrderStatus { New, Paid, Shipped, Cancelled }
// A Java enum constant is an object, not a number, so it can carry fields and methods.
public enum OrderStatus {
    NEW("waiting for payment"), PAID("being packed"), SHIPPED("on its way"), CANCELLED("cancelled");

    private final String label;
    OrderStatus(String label) { this.label = label; }   // always private
    public String label() { return label; }
}

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.valueOf("PAID");    // C#: Enum.Parse; throws if unknown
String statusLabel = status.label();                 // "being packed"
int position = status.ordinal();                     // 1: only its position; never store it
// No cast from int and no [Flags]: use an EnumSet. For a map keyed by enum, use EnumMap.
What erasure takes away
// C#: public class InMemoryRepository<T> where T : IHasId
public interface HasId { long id(); }
public class InMemoryRepository<T extends HasId> {       // the constraint goes in the brackets
    private final Map<Long, T> items = new HashMap<>();
    public void save(T item) { items.put(item.id(), item); }
    // Java erases type arguments when it compiles, so at run time T is unknown.
    // public T blank() { return new T(); }              // does not compile
}
// So APIs take a Class<T>: mock(OrderRepository.class). C#: typeof(T) just works.
// A type argument cannot be primitive: List<Integer>, never List<int>. Each element is boxed.
Variance is at the use site
// C#: IEnumerable<out T>. Java writes it where the type is used:
// ? extends for out, and ? super for in.
void printAll(List<? extends Payment> payments) { payments.forEach(System.out::println); }

List<Card> cards = List.of(new Card("4242"));
printAll(cards);                                 // prints Card[last4=4242]
// List<Payment> all = cards;                    // does not compile
Retention: the concept C# lacks
// C#: [Audited(Action = "refund")]. An annotation is Java's attribute.
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)              // without this, reflection cannot see it
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)                      // C#: AttributeUsage
public @interface Audited {
    String action();                             // members look like methods with no body
    String actor() default "system";
}
public class Refunds {
    @Audited(action = "refund")                  // arguments are written name = value
    public void refund(long orderId) { }
}

Audited audited = Refunds.class.getMethod("refund", long.class).getAnnotation(Audited.class);
String actor = audited.actor();                  // "system"
Optional is for return values
// Any reference can be null, and Java has no string?, no ?. and no ??.
// A method that may find nothing returns an Optional. Use it for return values only.
Optional<Customer> found = Optional.of(ada);     // Optional.empty() when there is none
String name = found.map(Customer::name).orElse("unknown");   // C#: found?.Name ?? "unknown"
String nickname = null;
String shown = Objects.requireNonNullElse(nickname, "none");  // "none"; C#: nickname ?? "none"
// orElse(x) always works out x. orElseGet(() -> x) does so only when empty.
JSpecify: the annotation standard
// C#: Invoice? Find(long orderId), checked by the compiler.
// JSpecify's annotations say the same, but only a checker such as NullAway enforces them.
public @Nullable Invoice findInvoice(long orderId) { return null; }
Creating collections
// C#: List<string> ids = ["mug", "cup", "pot"];
// Declare the interface and create the class. ArrayList is C#'s List<T>.
List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("mug", "cup", "pot"));
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();    // C#: Dictionary<string, int>
for (var i : ids) stock.put(i, 12);              // C#: foreach (var i in ids)
// Removing inside that loop usually throws. Call removeIf instead.
ids.removeIf(i -> i.startsWith("c"));
List<String> fixed = List.of("mug", "cup");      // cannot change, and rejects null
fixed.add("pot");                                // throws UnsupportedOperationException
3. Auto-unboxing throws NullPointerException
// C#: stock["jug"] throws KeyNotFoundException. Java's get returns null.
Integer missing = stock.get("jug");              // null
int unboxed = stock.get("jug");                  // throws NullPointerException
int safe = stock.getOrDefault("jug", 0);         // 0
13. Views are not copies
// subList, keySet, values and reversed() return views, not copies. C#'s list[0..1] copies.
List<String> view = ids.subList(0, 1);
view.set(0, "tray");
String first = ids.getFirst();                   // "tray": the change reached ids
2. The Integer cache
Integer a = 127, b = 127;                        // Integer is a boxed int. C#: int?, roughly
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
boolean small = a == b;                          // true: one shared object from -128 to 127
boolean large = c == d;                          // false: two objects, compared by reference
boolean equal = c.equals(d);                     // true: compare objects with equals
The equals and hashCode contract
// C#: override Equals and GetHashCode together. The same rule holds in Java,
// or a HashMap cannot find your key. A record writes both for you.
var shelves = new HashMap<OrderLine, String>();
shelves.put(line, "shelf 4");
String shelf = shelves.get(new OrderLine("mug", 2, new Money("9.50")));   // "shelf 4"
The shape
var orders = List.of(order, new Order(1043, ada, List.of(more, line), OrderStatus.NEW));
// C#: orders.Where(...).OrderByDescending(o => o.Id).Select(o => o.Id).ToList()
List<Long> newest = orders.stream()                          // a collection gives a stream
        .filter(o -> !o.lines().isEmpty())                   // Where
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::id).reversed())  // OrderByDescending
        .map(Order::id)                                      // Select
        .toList();                               // [1043, 1042]; this list cannot be modified
int units = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())        // SelectMany
        .mapToInt(OrderLine::quantity).sum();    // 7: sum() needs a stream of int
Collectors
// C#: orders.GroupBy(o => o.Status). In Java, grouping is a collector.
Map<OrderStatus, Long> byStatus = orders.stream().collect(groupingBy(Order::status, counting()));
String csv = ids.stream().collect(joining(", "));    // "tray, pot"; C#: string.Join
// toMap throws on a duplicate key, as ToDictionary does, and also on a null value.
Single use
// A stream can be used only once. A LINQ query would simply run again.
Stream<Order> paid = orders.stream().filter(o -> o.status() == OrderStatus.PAID);
long paidCount = paid.count();                   // 1: count() returns a long
paid.toList();                                   // throws IllegalStateException
// Leave parallelStream() alone: it shares one thread pool with the whole JVM.
Creating and running them
// C#: await Task.WhenAll(a, b). Java has no async and no await.
// Write blocking code and run it on a virtual thread, which makes waiting cheap.
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<String> who = executor.submit(() -> ada.name());           // C#: Task.Run
    Future<Integer> size = executor.submit(() -> order.lines().size());
    String report = who.get() + ": " + size.get();                    // "Ada Doe: 1"
}   // close() waits for every task
// Never pool virtual threads: to limit concurrency, use a Semaphore.
// They do not speed up calculation: use a sized pool of ordinary threads for that.
The problem it solves
// C#: await Task.WhenAll(a, b). A scope also cancels what is still running when
// its block ends. Structured concurrency is still a preview feature in Java 25:
// it needs --enable-preview to compile and to run, and its API changes between
// releases. So this stop is only a comment.
//   try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
//       var customer = scope.fork(() -> fetchCustomer(id));
//       var history = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrders(id));
//       scope.join();                           // waits, and throws the first failure
//       return merge(customer.get(), history.get());
//   }
// Until it is final, production code uses the executor above.
Cancellation is interruption
// C#: CancellationToken and OperationCanceledException. In Java, cancelling is interrupting.
Thread worker = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(30));    // C#: Task.Delay
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();      // catching clears the flag, so restore it
    }
});
worker.interrupt();
Mutual exclusion
// C#: lock (gate) { total += x; }
public class SalesTotal {
    private final Object gate = new Object();    // a private final lock object, never this
    private long total;

    public void add(int x) {
        synchronized (gate) { total += x; }
    }
}
Concurrent collections
// C#: ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd, which may run its factory more than once.
var prices = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Money>();
Money cached = prices.computeIfAbsent("mug", k -> new Money("9.50"));   // at most once per key
// AtomicInteger, shown above, and LongAdder replace C#'s Interlocked.
8. Integer overflow
// The primitives match C#'s, but byte is signed and there are no unsigned integers.
int wrapped = Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1;             // -2147483648: Java has no checked
Math.addExact(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1);             // throws ArithmeticException
byte signed = (byte) 200;                        // -56
Integer boxed = 42;                              // a wrapper object, which can be null. C#: int?
Money is BigDecimal
// C#: decimal sum = unit * 3 + 4.95m;
// Java has no decimal. BigDecimal is a class, so arithmetic is method calls.
double wrong = 0.1 + 0.2;                                    // 0.30000000000000004
BigDecimal unit = new BigDecimal("19.99");                   // from a string, never a double
BigDecimal sum = unit.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(3)).add(new BigDecimal("4.95"));    // 64.92
boolean over = sum.compareTo(new BigDecimal("50")) > 0;      // true: there is no > operator
boolean scale = new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00"));   // false: use compareTo
BigDecimal third = BigDecimal.ONE.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
// 0.33. Without a scale and a rounding mode, 1 divided by 3 throws ArithmeticException.
java.time
// Use java.time only. Its types cannot change and are safe to share between threads.
// Date, Calendar and SimpleDateFormat are the old API: read them, do not write them.
Instant now = Instant.now();                               // C#: DateTimeOffset, in UTC
LocalDate due = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 3).plusDays(30);    // 2026-11-02; C#: DateOnly
Duration wait = Duration.ofMinutes(90);                    // PT1H30M; C#: TimeSpan
// A Period is calendar time: a day, even when a clock change makes it 23 hours long.
Checked exceptions
// C# has only unchecked exceptions. A Java checked exception, such as IOException,
// must be declared or caught.
String read(Path path) throws IOException {      // declared: every caller has the same duty
    return Files.readString(path);
}
String readUnchecked(Path path) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(path);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException(e);       // wrapped; always keep the cause
    }
}
// RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked, such as IllegalStateException,
// which is C#'s InvalidOperationException.
9. Checked exceptions do not fit in lambdas
// A lambda passed to map cannot throw a checked exception. C# has no such limit.
List<Path> paths = List.of(Path.of("missing.txt"));
// paths.stream().map(Files::readString).toList();           // does not compile
List<String> texts = paths.stream().map(this::readUnchecked).toList();   // throws UncheckedIOException
try-with-resources
// C#: using (var gateway = new CardGateway()) { ... }
try (var gateway = new CardGateway()) {
    System.out.println(gateway.url);             // prints https://pay.example
}   // close() runs here, even on an exception
// url is protected, and this code is in the same package, so it can read it.
// catch (IOException | SQLException e) catches several types. Java has no when filter.
14. finally can swallow exceptions
int load() {
    try {
        throw new IllegalStateException("real problem");
    } finally {
        return 0;          // C# refuses to compile this. Java compiles it.
    }
}

int loaded = load();       // 0: the exception was silently discarded
The standard layout
// Maven is the build tool, and pom.xml is its .csproj. The layout is fixed:
//   pom.xml               names the project and lists its dependencies
//   src/main/java/        code, in folders that match the packages
//   src/main/resources/   application.yml and other files that go into the JAR
//   src/test/java/        tests, in the same packages as the code they test
// Sharing the package is how a test sees package-private members. C#: InternalsVisibleTo.
The lifecycle
//   ./mvnw clean package       compiles, tests, and builds the JAR in target/
//   ./mvnw test                C#: dotnet test
//   ./mvnw dependency:tree     shows which version of each library Maven chose
// ./mvnw is the wrapper: a script in the project that downloads the right Maven.
// C#: dotnet add package. Maven has no such command: paste a <dependency> into pom.xml.
A test
// JUnit, AssertJ and Mockito play the parts of xUnit, FluentAssertions and Moq.
class OrderServiceTest {                         // no public needed
    @Test                                        // C#: [Fact]
    void place_savesTheOrder() {
        OrderRepository repository = mock(OrderRepository.class);    // the mock is the object
        var service = new OrderService(repository);
        var line = new OrderLine("mug", 1, new Money("9.50"));
        var order = new Order(7, null, List.of(line), OrderStatus.NEW);

        assertThat(service.place(order)).isEqualTo(order);           // the actual value first
        verify(repository, times(1)).save(order);                    // C#: Verify(..., Times.Once)
    }
}

The tour was compiled with javac --release 25 on 3 October 2026, and every result shown in a comment was confirmed by running the code.

Spring Boot in 15 minutes#

Part TOURS · Quick tours · Chapter 54· 16 min read

This is one small order service on Spring Boot 4, from pom.xml to its tests, as a single listing in which the comments do the teaching. Read it from top to bottom. The link above each stop opens the section that explains it.

Starters
<!-- pom.xml: the parent sets compatible versions for hundreds of libraries. -->
<!-- ASP.NET Core: the .csproj, with its Sdk line and its PackageReference lines. -->
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.1</version>   <!-- current in September 2026; check spring.io -->
</parent>

<!-- A starter is one dependency that brings a whole capability, already set up. -->
<!-- It has no version, because the parent sets it. -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>   <!-- Boot 3: spring-boot-starter-web -->
</dependency>
<!-- This service also uses the starters data-jpa, validation, security, actuator and test. -->
The entry point
// BillingApplication.java
// ASP.NET Core: Program.cs, with WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args) and app.Run().
package com.acme.billing;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

// TRAP: Spring finds your classes by scanning this class's package and everything below it.
// A component in a sibling package is invisible, so keep this class in the root package.
@SpringBootApplication
public class BillingApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Creates the beans, starts the embedded web server, and runs until stopped.
        SpringApplication.run(BillingApplication.class, args);
    }
}
Auto-configuration
# Auto-configuration: each starter ships configuration classes that switch themselves on
# only when their conditions hold, such as "the JDBC classes are on the classpath".
# ASP.NET Core: no counterpart. You call builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>() yourself.
# Anything you define yourself wins: declare your own DataSource bean, and Boot's steps aside.
./mvnw spring-boot:run                        # dotnet run; the default port is 8080
./mvnw package                                # dotnet publish; builds one runnable JAR
java -jar target/billing-1.0.0.jar --debug    # --debug prints what Boot configured, and why
Configuration files
# src/main/resources/application.yml
# ASP.NET Core: appsettings.json. Here indentation shows nesting, instead of braces.
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost/billing
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false       # on by default; the stop on find() below says why it is off
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate      # Hibernate only checks the tables; the migrations build them
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true           # RFC 9457 error bodies, as AddProblemDetails(); off by default

billing:                      # your own settings can have any name
  max-lines: 50
Profiles are environments
# A profile is Spring's word for an environment.
# ASP.NET Core: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development and appsettings.Development.json
export SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev    # Boot also loads application-dev.yml, on top

# An environment variable beats both files. It is upper case, with one underscore.
# ASP.NET Core: Billing__MaxLines, with two underscores.
export BILLING_MAX_LINES=20          # sets billing.max-lines
IOptions becomes @ConfigurationProperties
// BillingProperties.java
// ASP.NET Core: IOptions<BillingOptions>. Here the record is injected itself, with no wrapper.
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "billing")        // binds the billing section of the settings
public record BillingProperties(int maxLines) { }   // max-lines fills maxLines

@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties(BillingProperties.class)   // creates the BillingProperties bean
class BillingConfig { }
An entity
// Order.java
// C#: an EF Core entity class. JPA maps it with annotations, not in OnModelCreating.
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

enum OrderStatus { NEW, PAID, SHIPPED, CANCELLED }

// TRAP: an entity cannot be a record. JPA needs a no-argument constructor and fields it can
// change, and Hibernate generates subclasses of entities. A record is final and immutable.
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")                    // ORDER is a reserved word in SQL
public class Order {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)   // the database generates the id
    private Long id;

    // TRAP: the default is ORDINAL, which stores the constant's position as a number.
    // Reorder the enum later, and every stored row silently means something different.
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.NEW;

    private Instant placedAt = Instant.now();   // the column is placed_at

    protected Order() { }                       // for JPA only
Lazy loading and detached entities
    // C#: navigation properties. In JPA a collection loads lazily by default.
    // TRAP: @ManyToOne is EAGER by default, so every order would load its customer.
    // Set LAZY every time.
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private Customer customer;

    // @OneToMany is LAZY by default: the lines load when they are first touched.
    // mappedBy names the field on OrderLine that holds the foreign key.
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    public Order(Customer customer, String productId, int quantity) {
        this.customer = customer;
        lines.add(new OrderLine(this, productId, quantity));   // saved with the order, by cascade
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public Customer getCustomer() { return customer; }
    public List<OrderLine> getLines() { return lines; }
    public OrderStatus getStatus() { return status; }
    public void cancel() { status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED; }
}
An entity
// OrderLine.java and Customer.java. C#: two more entity classes.
@Entity
class OrderLine {

    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private Order order;                   // the field that mappedBy = "order" names

    private String productId;
    private int quantity;

    protected OrderLine() { }

    OrderLine(Order order, String productId, int quantity) {
        this.order = order;
        this.productId = productId;
        this.quantity = quantity;
    }
}

@Entity
class Customer {

    @Id
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    protected Customer() { }

    public String getName() { return name; }
}
Repositories
// OrderRepository.java
// C#: a DbSet<Order>, queried with LINQ.
// Java has no expression trees, so Spring Data builds each query from the method's name.
import java.util.Optional;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.repository.query.Param;

// An interface with no implementation: Spring Data creates the class at startup.
// save, findById, findAll and delete are inherited.
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    // A derived query: where status = ? order by placed_at desc
    List<Order> findByStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc(OrderStatus status);

    // When the name would get silly, write the query. It names the entity and its fields,
    // not the tables. join fetch loads the lines in the same query.
    @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findWithLines(@Param("id") Long id);
The N+1 problem
    // TRAP, N+1: loop over findAll() and call order.getLines() on each order, and every
    // call runs a query. 100 orders cost 101 queries.
    // C#: .Include(o => o.Lines). Here @EntityGraph asks for the lines in the same query.
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines")
    List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);
}

interface CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long> { }
Migrations
-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__add_order_status.sql
-- ASP.NET Core: dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderStatus, then dotnet ef database update.
-- Flyway: you write plain SQL in numbered files. Boot runs each new file once, at startup.
ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW';
-- TRAP: Flyway stores a checksum of every file it applied. Edit one later, even to add a
-- comment, and startup fails. The fix for a mistake is always a new migration.
A record can be a document
// Invoice.java: a document, not a row. Suppose the invoices live in Amazon DocumentDB, which
// speaks the MongoDB API. Spring Data MongoDB stores each invoice whole, in a collection.
// C#: a class whose Id carries [BsonId] and [BsonRepresentation(BsonType.ObjectId)].
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.index.Indexed;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.Document;

// A document can be a record, which a JPA entity cannot.
// This @Id is Spring Data's own, spelled out because jakarta.persistence.Id is imported above.
// A String id is generated on saving. A long id is not.
@Document("invoices")
public record Invoice(
        @org.springframework.data.annotation.Id String id,
        // TRAP: no index exists, and nothing is enforced, until the setting
        // spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation is true.
        @Indexed(unique = true) String orderId,
        Money total,                       // a nested record is stored inside the document
        LocalDate issuedOn) { }

record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) { }
Repositories and derived queries
// InvoiceRepository.java: a repository again, this time over a collection.
// C#: IMongoCollection<Invoice> invoices = database.GetCollection<Invoice>("invoices");
//     await invoices.Find(i => i.OrderId == orderId).FirstOrDefaultAsync();
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.repository.MongoRepository;

public interface InvoiceRepository extends MongoRepository<Invoice, String> {

    // A derived query: it sends the filter {"orderId": orderId}.
    Optional<Invoice> findByOrderId(String orderId);
}

// In a service:
//     Invoice saved = invoices.save(invoice);
// TRAP: a record cannot change, so save returns a copy that carries the generated id.
// invoice.id() is still null. C#: InsertOneAsync sets Id on the object you passed.
Constraint annotations
// CreateOrder.java: the request body. A type that only carries data is a record.
// C#: record CreateOrder(long CustomerId, [Required] string ProductId, [Range(1, 100)] int Quantity);
import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public record CreateOrder(
        long customerId,
        // TRAP: @NotNull is not [Required] for a string, because it accepts "".
        // @NotBlank rejects null, empty and whitespace-only strings.
        @NotBlank String productId,
        @Min(1) @Max(100) int quantity) { }
Records as DTOs
// OrderDto.java: the response. Jackson, Spring's JSON library, reads and writes records.
// Boot 4 uses Jackson 3, in the package tools.jackson. Boot 3: com.fasterxml.jackson.
// C#: public record OrderDto(long Id, string Status, int LineCount);
public record OrderDto(long id, String status, int lineCount) {

    static OrderDto from(Order order) {
        return new OrderDto(order.getId(), order.getStatus().name(), order.getLines().size());
    }
}
Registration by annotation
// OrderService.java
// ASP.NET Core: builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();
// Spring has no registration list. The annotation is the registration.
// An object that Spring creates and hands to other objects is called a bean.
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;        // final is C#'s readonly
    private final CustomerRepository customers;
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;

    // Constructor injection: a class with one constructor needs no annotation for it.
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, CustomerRepository customers,
                        ApplicationEventPublisher events) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.customers = customers;
        this.events = events;
    }
Lifetimes: the default is singleton
// ASP.NET Core: you choose AddSingleton, AddScoped or AddTransient every time.
// TRAP: a bean is a singleton unless you say otherwise. There is one OrderService,
// so this field would be shared by every request:
//     private Order current;
// Keep beans stateless. @RequestScope is AddScoped; @Scope("prototype") is AddTransient.
The default
// C#: BeginTransaction, SaveChanges and Commit, with Rollback in a catch block.
// Spring starts a transaction before the method runs, commits when it returns,
// and rolls back when an unchecked exception escapes.
// Put it on the service, not the repository: the use case is the boundary.
@Transactional
public OrderDto place(CreateOrder request) {
    var customer = customers.findById(request.customerId()).orElseThrow();
    var order = orders.save(                 // db.Orders.Add(order)
            new Order(customer, request.productId(), request.quantity()));
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.getId()));   // see OrderPlacedListener below
    return OrderDto.from(order);
}
Lazy loading and detached entities
// C#: AsNoTracking() is the nearest thing to readOnly = true.
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public Optional<OrderDto> find(long id) {
    // Map to the DTO here, inside the transaction, while lazy fields can still load.
    return orders.findWithLines(id).map(OrderDto::from);
    // TRAP: return the Order instead, and order.getCustomer().getName() in the controller
    // throws LazyInitializationException, because the transaction has closed.
    // Boot's open-in-view hides that: it keeps the persistence context open for the
    // whole request. It also hides N+1 queries and holds a connection longer.
}

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<OrderDto> list(OrderStatus status) {
    return orders.findByStatus(status).stream().map(OrderDto::from).toList();
}
The rollback rule
// TRAP: only unchecked exceptions roll back. A checked exception COMMITS on the way out.
// C#: no counterpart. C# has no checked exceptions, so you have no instinct for this.
// OrderAlreadyShipped extends Exception, so it is checked. rollbackFor is the fix.
@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void cancel(long orderId) throws OrderAlreadyShipped {
    var order = orders.findById(orderId).orElseThrow();
    var shipped = order.getStatus() == OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
    order.cancel();      // no save call: the change to a loaded entity is written on commit
    if (shipped) throw new OrderAlreadyShipped();   // without rollbackFor, the cancel stays
}
Why self-invocation fails
    // TRAP: @Transactional is applied by a proxy, a stand-in object that wraps this one.
    // this::place calls the method on the object itself, so it never passes the proxy.
    // No transaction starts, and nothing warns you. A private method fails the same way.
    // C#: no counterpart. Nothing in ASP.NET Core wraps your class for you.
    public void placeAll(List<CreateOrder> requests) {
        requests.forEach(this::place);
    }
}

class OrderAlreadyShipped extends Exception { }

// The fix: make the call come from another bean, so that it goes through the proxy.
@Service
class BatchService {

    private final OrderService orders;

    BatchService(OrderService orders) { this.orders = orders; }

    public void placeAll(List<CreateOrder> requests) {
        requests.forEach(orders::place);     // one transaction for each order
    }
}
Two kinds of proxy
// What other classes receive is the proxy: a subclass that Spring generates at run time.
// C#: nothing does this for you. You write a decorator class and register it yourself.
import org.springframework.boot.ApplicationArguments;
import org.springframework.boot.ApplicationRunner;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
class ShowProxy implements ApplicationRunner {     // ASP.NET Core: IHostedService.StartAsync

    private final OrderService orders;

    ShowProxy(OrderService orders) { this.orders = orders; }

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {   // Boot calls this once, after startup
        System.out.println(orders.getClass().getName());
        // prints com.acme.billing.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
        // TRAP: a subclass cannot override a final method, so final on a @Transactional
        // method turns the transaction off, with only a warning in the startup log.
        // A final class stops startup: "Cannot subclass final class".
    }
}
Propagation
// Propagation: what happens when a transaction is already running.
// REQUIRED, the default, joins it. C#: TransactionScopeOption.RequiresNew for the one below.
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Propagation;

@Service
class AuditService {

    // REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller's transaction and commits on its own,
    // so the audit row survives when the caller rolls back.
    // TRAP: it takes a second connection from the pool. If it writes a row the caller
    // has already written, it waits for a lock that the caller cannot release.
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void record(String what) { }
}
Doing something after the commit
// TRAP: send a message inside place(), and it goes out even if the transaction rolls back.
// So place() publishes an event, and this listener runs only after the commit.
// C#: do the work after SaveChanges and Commit succeed.
import org.springframework.transaction.event.TransactionPhase;
import org.springframework.transaction.event.TransactionalEventListener;

record OrderPlaced(long orderId) { }

@Component
class OrderPlacedListener {

    // TRAP: an event published while no transaction is running is dropped.
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    public void on(OrderPlaced e) {
        // send the confirmation here
    }
}
A controller
// OrderController.java
// ASP.NET Core: [ApiController] [Route("orders")] class OrdersController : ControllerBase
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController                  // return values are written to the response body as JSON
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;

    public OrderController(OrderService orders) { this.orders = orders; }

    // GET /orders/{id}. ASP.NET Core: [HttpGet("{id}")] returning ActionResult<OrderDto>
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> get(@PathVariable long id) {   // text that is no number: 400
        return orders.find(id)
                .map(ResponseEntity::ok)                               // 200, as Ok(order)
                .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());   // 404, as NotFound()
    }
Model binding
// GET /orders?status=PAID. ASP.NET Core: [FromQuery] string status = "NEW"
// TRAP: @RequestParam is required by default. A request without it gets 400, not null.
// Give it a defaultValue, as here, or required = false.
@GetMapping
public List<OrderDto> list(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "NEW") String status) {
    return orders.list(OrderStatus.valueOf(status));   // returned directly: 200
}
Triggering validation
// POST /orders. ASP.NET Core: [HttpPost] with [FromBody]; [ApiController] validates for you.
// TRAP: forget @Valid and nothing checks CreateOrder's constraints, with no warning.
// With it, a bad body gets 400 Bad Request, and this method never runs.
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder request) {
    var created = orders.place(request);
    var location = URI.create("/orders/" + created.id());
    return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(created);   // 201, as CreatedAtAction
}
Method-level authorisation
    // ASP.NET Core: [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
    // TRAP: hasRole('ADMIN') checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN. hasAuthority adds no prefix.
    // TRAP: without @EnableMethodSecurity the annotation is silently ignored.
    // It is applied by a proxy too, so a call from inside the same class skips the check.
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> cancel(@PathVariable long id) throws OrderAlreadyShipped {
        orders.cancel(id);
        return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();   // 204, as NoContent()
    }
}
Global exception handling
// ApiExceptionHandler.java: one class gives every controller's exceptions an RFC 9457 body.
// ASP.NET Core: app.UseExceptionHandler(...), or an IExceptionFilter.
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.ResponseEntityExceptionHandler;

// Extending this class keeps Spring's bodies for its own exceptions, such as a failed @Valid.
// TRAP: that default body does not name the failing fields, where ASP.NET Core's does.
@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderAlreadyShipped.class)
    ProblemDetail handleShipped(OrderAlreadyShipped e) {
        var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "A shipped order cannot be cancelled");
        problem.setTitle("Order already shipped");
        return problem;      // status 409, with "title" and "detail" in the JSON
    }
}
The filter chain
// SecurityConfig.java. Spring Security is a chain of filters that every request passes
// through before it reaches a controller. One bean configures it.
// ASP.NET Core: AddAuthentication(), AddAuthorization(), UseAuthentication(), UseAuthorization()
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableMethodSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity                  // switches @PreAuthorize on
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean                              // the method's return value becomes a bean
    SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            // TRAP: rules are checked in order and the first match wins. anyRequest() goes last.
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()    // [AllowAnonymous]
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            // TRAP: CSRF protection is on by default, so a POST without its token gets 403.
            // Switch it off only for a token-based API that browsers do not call with cookies.
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
Concept mapping
            // ASP.NET Core: AddJwtBearer(), with Authority for the issuer.
            // Here the setting is spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri.
            // A token's scopes become authorities, such as SCOPE_orders.
            // TRAP: a "roles" claim is ignored until a JwtAuthenticationConverter bean maps it.
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .build();
    }
}
Actuator endpoints
# application.yml, continued. The actuator starter adds endpoints under /actuator.
# ASP.NET Core: AddHealthChecks(), for the health endpoint only.
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus   # only health is exposed by default
# TRAP: never expose env, heapdump, beans or configprops publicly.
# Boot 4 adds /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness by default.
Testing a controller
// OrderControllerTest.java
// ASP.NET Core: WebApplicationFactory<Program>, which starts the whole application.
// @WebMvcTest is a test slice: it starts the web layer with this one controller, and no database.
// Boot 4 moved it to the module spring-boot-webmvc-test, so its import differs from Boot 3.
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.*;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;              // sends requests with no real server or network

    @MockitoBean OrderService orders;    // a Mockito mock replaces the bean. Boot 3: @MockBean

    // TRAP: with Spring Security on the classpath, the slice protects every request.
    // Without a signed-in user this test gets 401, not 200.
    @Test
    @WithMockUser
    void get_returnsOrder() throws Exception {
        when(orders.find(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(new OrderDto(1, "PAID", 2)));

        mvc.perform(get("/orders/1"))
           .andExpect(status().isOk())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1));
        // An unstubbed find returns Optional.empty(), so the controller would answer 404.
    }
}
Full integration tests
// @SpringBootTest starts the real application context.
// ASP.NET Core: WebApplicationFactory<Program> again.
// TRAP: Boot 4 no longer provides MockMvc here. Boot 3 did.
// Without @AutoConfigureMockMvc, the test fails to start with "no qualifying bean".
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureMockMvc;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class OrderIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
}
Testing repositories
// @DataJpaTest starts JPA and the repositories, and nothing else.
// ASP.NET Core: no counterpart. Test slices do not exist there.
// TRAP: by default it swaps in an in-memory H2 database and rolls each test back.
// H2 does not behave like PostgreSQL, and the rollback hides errors that fire on commit.
// Replace.NONE keeps the real database, which the chapter starts in a container.
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.jdbc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.boot.jdbc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace;

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired OrderRepository orders;

    @Test
    void findsByStatus() {
        assertThat(orders.findByStatus(OrderStatus.PAID)).isEmpty();
    }
}
// Most tests should need no Spring at all. Constructor injection lets a plain JUnit test
// write new OrderService(...) with fakes, and such a test runs in milliseconds.
